2.3. Differences in Product Composition Among Pathways

The pathway-dependent differences in engine compatibility and downstream application performance originate primarily from differences in product molecular composition. The main differences lie in the proportions of n-paraffins, iso-paraffins, cycloalkanes, and aromatics [4]. HEFA, FT, and conventional ATJ routes generally produce fuels with a low aromatic content, whereas FT-SPK/A and ATJ-SKA routes improve specification matching by introducing aromatic components. The SIP route is mainly characterized by iso-paraffinic products [4].

As shown in Figure 1, the engineering differences among SAF pathways are rooted not only in feedstock origin and process route, but also in the resulting hydrocarbon-class distribution, which further affects cost, blend limit, and practical applicability.

For engine applications, a fuel should not be evaluated only according to whether it is labeled as HEFA-, FT-, ATJ-, or SIP-derived. These labels indicate the production route, while engine performance is influenced by the composition of the final fuel. From an engineering point of view, the more important issue is to study how each route affects the proportions of n-paraffins, iso-paraffins, cycloalkanes, and aromatics. For instance, cycloalkanes may increase fuel density and support seal swelling. However, highly branched iso-alkanes generally enhance the cold-flow properties, though this advantage might result in a lower density. Aromatics help preserve elastomer swelling, but they also promote soot formation and deposit precursors. Therefore, the balance of the fuel composition shows that the fuel design must not depend solely on the classification of the production route [50]. Landera et al. [50] investigated the relationship between structure and properties of cycloalkanes and found that the molecular structure has a significant influence on density, flash point, melting behavior, specific energy, and parameters related to seal swelling. Thus, the engineering value of cycloalkanes depends on their precise molecular structure rather than simply considering them as cyclic hydrocarbons. Boehm et al. [51] also emphasized that aviation fuel qualification requires probabilistic blending rules and a more thorough study of the composition and properties, since the linear blending assumptions frequently fail for complex non-petroleum fuel mixtures.

Recent fuel design studies reach a similar conclusion. The differences in paraffinic components can affect compliance with the standards, particularly concerning the freezing point, density, and aromatic control [52]. Webber et al. [52] showed that ETJ-derived hydrocarbons with higher iso-alkane content improve the cold flow property and facilitate the dispersion of high freezing point aromatic fractions, which is advantageous for meeting Jet A-1 standards. Dagle et al. [53] also suggested that the jet fuel mixtures containing mono- and bicycloalkanes together with iso-alkanes can increase the energy density, satisfy the freeze-point and flash-point requirements, and possibly assist in seal swelling. For future SAF design, coordinated control of cycloalkane and iso-alkane fractions is therefore likely to be more important than increasing either component class in isolation.

Klimczyk et al. [4] further emphasized that fuels generated from different pathways differ significantly in n-paraffin, iso-paraffin, cycloalkane, and aromatic content, and these compositional differences further affect key properties such as density, viscosity, flash point, cold flow properties, and material compatibility. In high SAF concentration or complex multicomponent fuel systems, simple component additivity often fails to reflect actual property changes accurately because such systems frequently show clear nonlinear behavior [54].

Accordingly, the essential differences among SAF pathways are first expressed as differences in molecular composition, and these in turn determine key fuel properties such as density, cold-flow properties, emissions behavior, and material compatibility [54]. This is precisely what affects their compatibility with aero-engines.

2.4. Basic Physicochemical Characteristics of SAF

In addition to pathway-dependent hydrocarbon class distribution, SAF application also depends on several basic physicochemical characteristics of the finished fuel or blending component [54]. These characteristics include elemental composition, density, viscosity, net heat of combustion, and freezing point, which are directly related to fuel specification compliance and engine applicability [6]. Because SAF is produced by different routes and may be used either as a neat blending component or as a finished blended fuel, these properties should be interpreted as pathway- and formulation-dependent rather than as fixed values for all SAFs [55]. Table 2 summarizes ASTM specification limits, representative reported data, and engineering implications of these key characteristics.

Overall, these properties show that SAF suitability cannot be judged only from feedstock origin or nominal pathway classification. The final fuel must combine low-carbon potential with sufficient density, energy content, low-temperature operability, and compositional cleanliness to meet aviation fuel specifications [6].

3. SAF Compatibility with Aero-Engines

3.1. Basis for Direct Drop-In Use in Current Aero-Engines

ASTM D1655 and ASTM D7566 provide the main specification framework for conventional aviation turbine fuels and aviation turbine fuels containing synthesized hydrocarbons, including requirements related to composition, volatility, fluidity, combustion performance, corrosion, thermal stability, contaminants, and additives. Whether SAF can enter the current aviation system therefore depends on whether the finished fuel remains compatible with this specification framework and with aero-engine combustion requirements [51,59].

From the perspective of gas turbine operation, SAF compatibility should be assessed along the complete fuel-to-combustor pathway rather than by comparing isolated bulk fuel properties alone. In a gas turbine engine, liquid fuel is stored, pumped, metered, heated in the fuel system, and injected into the combustor, where atomization, evaporation, mixing with compressed air, ignition, flame stabilization, heat release, and pollutant formation occur [59,60]. Changes in SAF density and net heat of combustion may affect fuel metering, required volumetric fuel flow, and range-related fuel loading. For example, Walkling et al. reported that HEFA-Jet had a higher net heat of combustion than Jet A, 43.73 MJ kg−1 compared with 43.1 MJ kg−1, but a lower density, 0.762 g mL−1 compared with 0.807 g mL−1 [7]. This indicates that gravimetric energy content and volumetric fuel loading may change in different directions. Viscosity, volatility, surface tension, and distillation characteristics influence spray breakup, droplet evaporation, ignition, high-altitude relight, and combustor stability margins [59]. Molecular composition, particularly the hydrogen-to-carbon ratio, aromatic content, and sulfur content, affects soot formation and particulate emissions [57,60]. Aromatic and cycloalkane fractions may also influence flame radiation, material compatibility, and other combustor-relevant behavior, and should therefore be assessed on a pathway-specific basis [59,60]. In addition, gas turbine engines use fuel not only as an energy carrier but also as a thermal management fluid. Fuel thermal stability and coking tendency are therefore important because deposits in injectors, manifolds, fuel nozzles, or heat exchangers can disturb fuel distribution, increase pressure drop, degrade atomization quality, and compromise long-term operational reliability [60,61]. Because fuel composition and fuel heat uptake may influence combustor exit conditions and thermal management requirements, their effects should also be assessed at the engine system level [61]. Therefore, SAF use in gas turbine engines should be evaluated through coupled operational criteria, including fuel system delivery, fuel control response, combustor operability, ignition and relight, combustion efficiency, emissions, thermal stability, resistance to coking, material compatibility, and durability under realistic engine operating conditions.

Recent evaluations indicate that the application of SAF in aero-engines should be evaluated by considering the integrated behavior of atomization, ignition, flame development, emission, and combustor operability rather than comparing their individual properties [59]. Ruan et al. [59] showed that the substitutability of the fuel depends largely on the interaction between the fuel composition and the combustion behavior, especially the spray atomization, ignition, flame speed, and soot production.

For basic fuel properties, Fossi et al. [62] reported that synthetic paraffinic kerosene obtained through the Fischer–Tropsch process had lower density, lower viscosity, and higher volatility than Jet A-1. These characteristics are favorable for low-temperature ignition and high-altitude restart. Walkling et al. [7] examined several bio-based candidate fuels and their blends with HEFA-Jet and Jet A, considering factors such as density, low-temperature viscosity, net heat of combustion, flash point, thermal stability, smoke point, and distillation behavior. Some of these compositions have already satisfied the important criteria of ASTM D7566.

In terms of spray and atomization characteristics, Lin et al. [63] studied the spray penetration distance, spray cone angle and spray volume of SAF in a constant volume combustion chamber, and found that ambient temperature, injection pressure, and ambient pressure have a significant influence on the spray behavior of SAF.

Flame speed and extinction data have been considered in the study of combustion reactivity. Abi Nurazaq et al. [64] examined the properties of SAF, Jet A-1, and JP-5 under high-pressure premixed conditions. The laminar flame speed of JP-5 was found to be the highest, while the difference between SAF and Jet A-1 was usually less than 15%, indicating that some SAFs have a combustion reactivity similar to that of conventional aviation fuels. Munzar et al. [65] presented the laminar flame speed, extinction stretch rate, and vapor pressure data for Jet A-1 and the hydroprocessed renewable jet fuel blends, which provides a basis for the systematic characterization of the reactivity of SAF blends.

For soot and deposit formation, Irimiea et al. [66] investigated high-pressure kerosene and SAF combustion and reported reduced soot formation under the tested SAF conditions. These findings suggest that some SAFs may reduce the formation of deposit precursors in high-pressure combustion environments. In engine-scale tests, Jarin et al. [67] examined the Jet A-1 and HEFA-based SAF in a MAKILA 2B turboshaft engine. Because the tested SAF had a higher hydrogen-to-carbon ratio and no aromatics, the CO2 emissions were reduced and the smoke number decreased by about 60%. Other turbine engine results also demonstrate that fuels containing HEFA can reduce particulate emissions under practical operating conditions [68]. Song et al. [57] analyzed the emissions of SAFs and conventional aviation fuels and found that SAFs usually decrease sulfur-containing emissions and particulate matter, whereas the changes in NOx are mainly influenced by the combustor design and operating conditions rather than the replacement of fuel alone.

Material compatibility is still an independent problem. Hamilton et al. [69] examined several elastomer sealing materials, which were exposed to conventional Jet A, HEFA-SAF, and ATJ-SAF in aviation fuel systems. Overall, the existing data indicate the technical possibility of SAF in terms of fuel properties, spray behavior, flame propagation, emissions, and material compatibility. However, significant variations exist among different SAF processes. Further research is required to demonstrate that the candidate fuels can satisfy the specifications of aviation turbine fuel and maintain stable spray combustion and reliable fuel system compatibility.

3.2. Influence of Low-Aromatic Composition on Emissions and Material Compatibility

A common characteristic of many mainstream SAF pathways is their low aromatic content [4]. This feature leads to improvements in particulate emissions and in the environmental effects associated with contrail formation. Flight measurements by Märkl et al. [70] in 2024 showed that, compared with Jet A-1, 100% HEFA-SPK reduced the number of ice crystals formed per unit mass of fuel by 56% under cruise conditions. The same study also reported a 35% reduction in the median non-volatile particulate matter emission index.

As shown in Figure 2, the reduction in soot-related particulate emissions is associated with a lower apparent ice emission index, which helps explain the reduced contrail ice crystal formation observed for 100% HEFA-SPK.

These findings show that low-aromatic, low-soot fuels affect not only engine exhaust particles but also the formation of high-altitude contrails.

In contrast, Dey et al. [60] noted that many synthetic SAFs, because of their low aromatic content, may weaken the swelling effect required by conventional elastomeric sealing materials, thereby creating material compatibility risks. Dey et al. [60] further noted that one of the key barriers to high-blend SAF application is that low-aromatic systems still face practical limitations in seal-material adaptation.

Recent experimental studies have provided more direct evidence that the compatibility problem of low-aromatic SAFs is closely related to the swelling behavior of nitrile-based sealing materials [71]. Faulhaber et al. [71] measured nitrile rubber absorption in a large set of neat molecules, blend components, and fuel mixtures and showed that O-ring swelling is strongly dependent on hydrocarbon composition, particularly the presence of aromatic and other swell-inducing species. More recent work by Luning Prak et al. [72] further showed that both commercial Buna-N O-rings and additively manufactured O-rings exhibit composition-dependent changes in swelling behavior and tensile strength after exposure to synthetic and surrogate fuel mixtures, which suggests that material compatibility should be evaluated not only in terms of volumetric swell but also in terms of mechanical integrity after fuel exposure.

As illustrated in Figure 3, the seal-swelling behavior is strongly influenced by composition, which confirms that the compatibility of low-aromatic SAF should be judged by the swelling margin instead of considering only the aromatic content. For the qualification of 100% SAF in the future, the aromatic content cannot be used as the sole criterion for evaluating compatibility. The detailed fuel chemistry and the behavior of particular elastomer materials also need to be investigated.

These findings suggest that the challenge of low-aromatic SAFs is not limited to simple seal shrinkage but also involves broader material property changes that may affect long-term fuel system reliability [71,72]. The current literature therefore suggests that the main reasons behind blend ratio limits can now be understood primarily in terms of two constraints: material compatibility and final fuel specification compliance.

3.3. Pathways Toward 100% SAF

The transition from high-blend SAF to 100% SAF should be treated as a system compatibility challenge rather than a simple increase in blending ratio [60]. In this review, “high-blend SAF” is used only as a review-specific working term, not as a formal ASTM fuel category. Unless otherwise stated, it refers to finished aviation turbine fuel containing roughly 20–50 vol% of an ASTM D7566 synthesized blending component. For pathways whose ASTM-approved blend limit is below 20%, the term refers to blends close to their pathway-specific approved maximum blend ratio rather than to a universal concentration threshold. The pathway-specific maximum blend ratios follow ASTM and ICAO pathway information [6,73]. Dey et al. [60] argued that achieving high-blend or even 100% SAF application requires the simultaneous solution of fuel composition optimization, material compatibility, and combustion/emissions control. The flight study by Märkl et al. [70] showed that the tested 100% HEFA-SPK provided a measurable non-CO2 climate benefit relative to the reference Jet A-1 under the investigated cruise conditions.

The ICAO technical update on 100% SAF testing progress [74] reported that in recent years, engine manufacturers and aviation stakeholders have carried out multiple ground and flight tests using 100% SAF. The ICAO technical briefing summarizes progress by Rolls-Royce and others on engine compatibility with 100% SAF and emphasizes that the purpose of these tests is to demonstrate that there are no fundamental technical barriers for current and in-production engines [74]. Chojnowski et al. [75] further noted that the widespread use of 100% SAF will require either the introduction of synthetic aromatic components to provide the necessary swelling behavior or the certification of sealing materials that are compatible with fully paraffinic fuel systems.

In addition to seal swelling, recent studies have shown that 100% paraffinic SAFs may also introduce other system-level compatibility issues beyond conventional material adaptation [76]. Yang et al. [76] identified the effect of fuel composition on dielectric constant as one challenge in developing 100% SAF because modern aircraft frequently rely on capacitance-based fuel gauging systems and differences in dielectric behavior between conventional jet fuel and highly paraffinic SAF can affect fuel quantity measurement accuracy.

The transition to 100% SAF is more than a combustion or elastomer compatibility problem; it also involves fuel-gauging compatibility, certification, and operational reliability [76]. Recent engine-scale research has also shown that 100% HEFA can achieve promising operating and emissions performance under turbofan-related conditions, which suggests that the technical route toward high blend and neat SAF use is still developing [77]. Xu et al. [77] reported that 100% HEFA could reduce emissions while maintaining stable engine operating characteristics in a small-scale turbofan, although further work is still needed to confirm material compatibility and physical property matching in unmodified commercial aircraft fuel systems. The transition to 100% SAF should therefore be treated as an integrated process that combines fuel composition optimization, seal material adaptation, fuel system instrumentation compatibility, and continuous engine-level verification [76,77].

As depicted in Figure 4, the main problem is not only the benefit of using low-aromatic SAF but also how to balance its emission and climate advantages with seal compatibility, the match of finished fuel properties and fuel system adaptability. This statement also clarifies why the change to 100% SAF should be considered as a coordinated issue including fuel composition, materials, sensing compatibility and certification instead of a simple substitution of fuel.

Based on the evidence summarized above, pathways toward 100% SAF appear feasible in principle for selected test fuels and specified combinations of engines and fuel systems, but they have not yet been demonstrated or approved across all SAF pathways, neat paraffinic blending components, aircraft fuel systems, and commercial operating scenarios [6,70,74,77]. The key point is that universal drop-in feasibility depends on the properties of the final fully formulated fuel rather than on those of a single neat synthetic blending component [6,60]. Such fuels must meet aviation turbine fuel specifications and combustion-operability requirements [6,60,77]. They must also provide adequate elastomer compatibility [71,72] and maintain the accuracy of aircraft fuel quantity-indicating systems [76]. Compliance with the specified thermal oxidation stability requirements must also be demonstrated [6].

Current evidence from flight demonstrations and engine tests indicates that selected 100% HEFA-based fuels can sustain engine operation under the tested conditions [70,74,77]. However, broader implementation still requires pathway-specific fuel formulation, including synthetic aromatic components or other composition-adjustment strategies where property matching and seal swelling are required [60,71,72]. Compatible sealing materials and validation of fuel system sensing may also be necessary [71,72,76], together with continued pathway-specific fuel qualification and aircraft, engine, and flight testing [6,74,77]. Therefore, 100% SAF should be regarded as technically feasible in selected cases, while its practical deployment remains a staged process involving fuel formulation, verification of material compatibility and validation of fuel system sensing, engine testing, flight demonstration, and certification.

Based on the available literature, the pathways toward 100% SAF can be summarized into three main categories. First, fuel-side solutions, namely the introduction of synthetic aromatics or optimization of molecular composition to compensate for the deficiencies of fully paraffinic SAF in seal swelling and some finished fuel properties. Second, material-side solutions, namely the development or certification of sealing materials and fuel system components that do not depend on aromatic swelling, so that existing fuel systems can operate under 100% SAF conditions. Third, standard- and certification-side solutions, namely the expansion of ASTM and airworthiness validation to more engines and fuel pathways, reduce the institutional barriers to full ratio application.

4. Property Prediction and Mechanistic Understanding of SAF

Property prediction and a mechanistic understanding are essential for SAF research because the engineering performance of SAF is ultimately controlled by the relationship between molecular composition, physicochemical properties, and end-use behavior [54]. Different SAF pathways produce different proportions of n-paraffins, iso-paraffins, cycloalkanes, and aromatics, which further influence density, viscosity, freezing point, flash point, thermal stability, emissions, and material compatibility [50,54]. For emerging SAF candidates, full experimental qualification is expensive, time-consuming, and often limited by small sample availability; therefore, reliable prediction methods are needed for early stage screening and blend optimization [78,79]. More importantly, property prediction should not only provide numerical estimates but also clarify why specific molecular structures or component classes lead to certain fuel behaviors [80]. In this regard, SAF property research is progressing from empirical property prediction to mechanistic interpretation, uncertainty quantification, and performance-oriented fuel design [81].

4.1. Limitations of Traditional Property Prediction Methods

With more studies on high-blend and complex multicomponent SAF systems, the traditional property prediction methods, which rely on component additivity or empirical mixing rules, are becoming more evident in their limitations [54].

Batool et al. [54] stated that although conventional empirical methods are still useful for simple systems, they usually cannot accurately describe the nonlinear characteristics of key properties such as density, viscosity, specific energy, flash point, and thermal stability in complicated SAF blends. Their survey also revealed that the property changes in high-SAF-concentration blends do not always obey linear superposition, thus leading to considerable errors in the simple empirical models. Oh et al. [78] indicated that SAF property prediction is often influenced by the lack of sufficient training data and the uncertainties in the compositional features, which limits the extrapolation ability of the empirical models. Similarly, Yang et al. [79] found in their GC×GC prescreening study for SAF candidates that properties such as density and flash point are easier to predict, while properties such as freezing point and viscosity are more affected by the compositional variations. This result indicates the limited applicability of conventional methods in complicated SAF systems.

Under high-blend SAF conditions, property prediction therefore cannot depend entirely on conventional empirical models.

4.2. Molecular Dynamics-Based Prediction of Thermophysical Properties

Besides the usual empirical methods, molecular dynamics (MD) provides a detailed route for predicting the properties of SAF and surrogate fuel systems. Batool et al. [54] showed that MD has been extensively used to model the thermophysical properties of SAF and other alternative fuel systems such as density, viscosity, thermal conductivity and heat capacity. One of the main advantages of MD is its capability to depict the liquid-phase structure, intermolecular interactions and the effects of temperature and pressure at the molecular level. Batool et al. further stated that, in the reported MD studies, the OPLS-AA force field usually gives satisfactory accuracy for liquid hydrocarbon systems. Liao et al. [82] carried out systematic simulations for density, thermal conductivity, and viscosity with TraPPE-UA and OPLS force fields and found that TraPPE-UA performed better in predicting density and thermal conductivity, while OPLS showed better results in viscosity prediction.

4.3. Data-Driven Methods and Uncertainty Quantification

Alongside molecular simulation, data-driven methods have become one of the fastest-growing areas of SAF property prediction. Their practical role is to identify key properties when only small sample sets and short evaluation windows are available, thereby supporting mixture optimization and preliminary verification [83].

The reason for using data-driven methods in SAF research is mainly practical rather than only computational. In practice, only small quantities of new SAF candidates are often available, but full fuel qualification requires extensive and costly experimental testing. A rapid screening model can therefore assist in deciding which candidate fuels require further experimental study. In this situation, the GC×GC, FTIR spectra, molecular descriptors, and other measured properties can be used as complementary inputs rather than separate datasets.

Figure 5 illustrates this procedure. The ultimate outcome is not only a calculated value for density, viscosity, flash point, or freezing point. A better model should also indicate which influencing factors affect the calculation and the error of the prediction. This is particularly important for SAF because the available training data are still insufficient and various possible fuels have different compositions from conventional petroleum-based jet fuels.

However, the reliability of these workflows depends mainly on the quality, diversity, and coverage of the training data. For SAF systems with limited experimental datasets, uncertainty quantification and mechanistic interpretability are therefore essential for avoiding overfitting and improving confidence in property prediction.

Li et al. [84] earlier proposed an ML-QSPR framework for multiple fuel types, establishing a database containing 1797 pure compounds and 465 mixtures and using machine learning models to predict 15 physicochemical properties. Their work demonstrated the feasibility of large-scale property prediction based on molecular descriptors. Shao et al. [85] further developed a composition–property database for 104 jet fuels and applied machine learning QSPR models to predict density, viscosity, net heat of combustion, freezing point, and flash point, showing that the key physicochemical properties of complex jet fuel systems can now be modeled effectively on the basis of relatively large datasets. Oh et al. [78] used a Bayesian neural network ensemble to perform deep uncertainty quantification for the relationship between GC×GC features and flash point, showing that insufficient training data and limited resolution compositional descriptors lead to epistemic and heteroscedastic uncertainty, respectively. This indicates that SAF property prediction should not be reduced to a single point estimate but should explicitly include confidence ranges and uncertainty source identification. Comesana et al. [83] demonstrated another promising route by combining liquid phase FTIR spectroscopy with machine learning and non-negative matrix factorization to extract interpretable spectral features for the prediction of final boiling point, flash point, freezing point, density, and kinematic viscosity. Their study shows that spectroscopic methods with smaller sample numbers, shorter acquisition times, and greater feature interpretability may also be effective as early stage screening tools for SAF.

Recent studies point to clear progress; data-driven SAF modeling is moving from simple accuracy-focused prediction toward models that also emphasize interpretability and uncertainty under data-scarce conditions.

4.4. From Property Prediction to Fuel Prescreening and Molecular Design

SAF property prediction is no longer used simply to replace experiments. It now supports fuel prescreening, formulation optimization and inverse molecular design.

The GC×GC-based prescreening tool developed by Yang et al. [79] indicated that small sample volumes are sufficient for rapid evaluation of several important combustor-operability and applicability indices, which is important from an engineering standpoint for the screening of new SAF candidates at an early stage. The review by Batool et al. [54] also suggests that component-based estimation, molecular simulation, and data-driven methods should not be regarded as alternative approaches. Rather, they form a complementary framework in which empirical methods are useful for rapid preliminary screening, molecular dynamics (MD) offers mechanistic understanding and supplementary property estimation under high-temperature and high-pressure conditions, and machine learning can support multi-property prediction in large data sets or high-dimensional feature spaces. The broader objective of SAF property prediction and mechanistic study is to explain existing fuels while also supporting new-fuel formulation, blend optimization, and targeted fuel development for specific engines or thermal-management needs.

SAF property research is also moving beyond individual physicochemical-property prediction toward end-use engine performance and emission behavior [80]. Kroyan et al. showed that variations in key SAF properties can produce measurable changes in engine fuel consumption and emission-related outputs, making property prediction an important basis for applicability assessment [80]. Future SAF property studies should therefore connect fuel composition, thermophysical properties and propulsion system behavior, rather than focus only on single-property prediction [80].

Recent advances in artificial intelligence have opened a route from property prediction to fuel-oriented design [81]. Freitas et al. presented a probabilistic deep-learning model for sustainable fuel design, showing that data-driven techniques can be used for both forward prediction and inverse exploration of candidate fuels with target property distributions and uncertainty limits [81]. Compared with conventional deterministic machine learning methods, this probabilistic perspective is better suited to SAF systems because it reflects uncertainty, compositional diversity, and coupling among multiple target properties [81].

The next step for SAF property prediction is likely to be an integrated framework that combines multi-property prediction, uncertainty quantification, performance selection, and inverse molecular or formulation design [80,81].

5. Heat Sink Demands of SAF in Aerospace Propulsion Systems

5.1. Fuel Heat Sink Demand and System-Level Thermal Management

With the development of high-Mach number aerospace propulsion systems, fuel becomes increasingly important as both an energy source and a coolant [86]. In high-thermal-load propulsion systems, in addition to supplying combustion energy, the fuel must flow through high-temperature walls, injection systems, or other local hot regions before entering the combustor, which can reduce structural heat load and enhance the system heat sink capacity [87]. SAF heat sink characteristics therefore need to be considered. However, direct data for specific SAFs under regenerative cooling conditions remain scarce, so studies on Jet A, RP-3, endothermic hydrocarbon fuels, and surrogate fuels should be used cautiously as mechanistic references rather than as direct evidence for SAF performance.

As illustrated in Figure 6, the heat sink capacity of fuel arises not only from its heat capacity but also from its role as a circulating heat sink in connecting wall cooling, fuel heating, and downstream combustion processes.

Recent studies of aircraft fuel thermal management systems indicate that the heat sink capacity of fuel is not merely a passive property but a system-level resource mainly influenced by the flow path design, subsystem arrangement, and heat load distribution [88,89]. Yang et al. [88] revealed that the thermal dissipation performance of an aircraft fuel thermal management system can be greatly enhanced by the optimal flow path design of the fuel, suggesting that the effective heat sink capacity of the fuel is closely associated with the system structure instead of solely the fuel properties. Xu et al. [89] proposed an optimization method for the aircraft fuel thermal management structures and demonstrated that the subsystem arrangement and the heat-exchanger configuration have a significant impact on the heat sink efficiency throughout the entire system. A hydrocarbon fuel precooler study for hypersonic engines shows that high heat sink hydrocarbon fuels can serve as the cold source, while fuel mass flow rate, air outlet temperature, tube bundle arrangement, and tube pitch govern precooler performance [90]. From a wider viewpoint, Guo et al. [91] emphasized that the future aero-engines and aircraft thermal management systems will need to handle the propulsion heat loads, onboard electrical loads, and fuel system heat dissipation together within a comprehensive energy thermal framework. Moreover, Dey et al. [60] stressed that the application of SAF in gas turbine engines should be considered not only in terms of combustion efficiency, emissions, and soot characteristics but also from the suitability for thermal management and high-temperature thermal stresses. Boehm et al. [61] additionally suggested that fuels with better thermal stability can allow engines to rely more on fuel as a heat sink and decrease the reliance on compressor bleed air cooling, thus possibly improving the propulsion-system efficiency. Experimental studies on compact aero-engine heat exchangers support this system-level view. Recent studies on serpentine tube heat exchangers for aero-engine cooling have evaluated compact hardware in terms of airside pressure drop and convective heat transfer [92,93]. A compact finned-tube air fuel heat exchanger test reached a similar conclusion: rectangular finned tube bundles increased heat-transfer area, but the outside convective heat-transfer coefficient was only about 44% of that of a comparable bare tube bundle, with higher flow resistance [94].

These findings indicate that in advanced aerospace propulsion systems, the function of fuel as a cooling agent should be evaluated together with the overall thermal management of the aircraft and engines, rather than merely as a local cooling effect in the combustor. In high-thermal load propulsion systems, the heat sink capacity of fuel has become an important factor in assessing the technical feasibility of SAF.

5.2. Active Regenerative Cooling and Fuel Thermal Stability

Active regenerative cooling is one of the most representative fuel-based thermal management strategies in high-thermal load propulsion systems. Its basic concept is to allow the fuel to flow through passages near high-temperature components before entering the combustor, so that heat can be absorbed, wall temperature can be reduced, and the heat sink capability of the fuel can be more effectively utilized [87].

Boehm et al. [61] reported that alternative aviation fuels with high thermal stability and low viscosity may increase the degree to which fuel can be used as a heat sink and reduce reliance on compressor bleed air cooling, thereby improving engine efficiency. The same study further showed that, if the maximum allowable fuel temperature is increased by approximately 50 °F, direct waste heat recovery alone may provide an energy saving of about 0.2%, while the benefit associated with higher thermal stability may account for about 60% of the total efficiency gain exceeding 0.5%. Thermal stability and resistance to coking are key indicators that determine whether a fuel can operate reliably in high-temperature fuel systems, and they are also basic criteria for judging whether a fuel is suitable for high-thermal load propulsion environments [61]. Yang et al. [95] showed that the heat-generation characteristics of the aero-engine fuel system are strongly coupled with aircraft-level thermal management demands, which means that the regenerative cooling performance of the fuel system depends on the broader distribution of thermal loads across the platform. In addition, recent work on fuel heat sink enhancement shows that optimization of the fuel tank and fuel circulation process can improve the overall thermal management capability of the aircraft fuel system, indicating that active regenerative cooling performance is influenced by both local channel heat transfer and upstream fuel-side thermal conditioning [96]. Future analyses of active regenerative cooling should place greater emphasis on integrated fuel system heat generation, tank-side heat sink management, and platform-level thermal matching, rather than focusing only on downstream cooling passages [95,96].

Sung et al. tested alternative aviation fuels using an experimental rig designed for coolant-like conditions and found that some 100% biogenic blended fuels could maintain good thermal stability and low coke deposition levels under high-temperature heating conditions. Their results showed that several 100% biogenic blended fuels all achieved the highest JFTOT rating, code 1, with zero pressure drop, indicating that these fuels already satisfy the thermal oxidation stability requirements of current aviation fuel specifications. Sung et al. [86] further showed that the deposit thickness of 100% biogenic blended fuels in thermal stability tests was only 6.39–9.72 nm, significantly lower than the 32.03 nm and 47.18 nm observed for two Jet A-containing comparison fuels. Under the tested conditions, this suggests that such high ratio biogenic fuels had clearly better coking resistance than conventional fuel-containing systems. Sung et al. also argued that the lower coke deposition level was likely related to the absence of aromatics in the 100% biogenic fuels, because aromatic species tend to participate more readily in deposit-precursor formation. This study therefore indicates that such fuels already have an experimental basis for entering active regenerative cooling scenarios. Related tests on an air fuel heat exchanger further show that a gradually thicker coke layer can increase thermal stress and contribute to tube failure, whereas secondary flow in bent tubes can improve convective heat transfer performance and reduce coke deposition [97].

5.3. Supercritical Regenerative Cooling: Heat Transfer, Pyrolysis, and System-Level Constraints

In addition, for high-thermal load propulsion systems, fuel system operating pressures typically reach 3.45–6.89 MPa, which often exceeds the critical pressure of typical hydrocarbon fuels. As a result, the fuel during active regenerative cooling usually undergoes transcritical or even supercritical states [98]. Previous investigations have shown that thermophysical properties change sharply as the fuel approaches and crosses the pseudo-critical region at supercritical pressure. These variations may cause heat transfer deterioration, flow instability, and uneven flow distribution, thereby reducing cooling effectiveness [99,100]. Zhang et al. [101] also presented a working state map for endothermic hydrocarbon fuels, which demonstrates that the supercritical region has become an important operating condition in the study of regenerative cooling, and its position varies with the heat flux and mass flow rate. Recent RP-3 measurements provide direct property data for this regime; isobaric specific heat capacity, viscosity, and density show clear behavior that depends on temperature and pressure in the transcritical temperature regions or under supercritical pressures [102,103,104]. Frictional resistance experiments further show that frictional pressure drop and friction factor vary with inlet temperature, heat flux and mass flux, and that the friction factor decreases suddenly when the fuel outlet temperature exceeds the pseudo-critical temperature [105]. These findings indicate that cooling channel analysis should consider hydraulic resistance together with thermophysical property variations.

Figure 7 applies the working state map framework to RP-3 using its reported critical and cracking-onset temperatures [98,101,106]. Before cracking begins, RP-3 lies in the subcritical or supercritical regime, and cooling is dominated by physical heat absorption. As the thermal load increases, the fuel approaches the cracking-onset temperature of approximately 900 K. Subsequent pyrolysis provides additional chemical heat sink but may also increase gas formation and coke deposition. The risking boundary is system dependent because it varies with wall-material limits, channel geometry, operating pressure, and heat-flux distribution. For SAF, this map should be interpreted as a mechanistic reference because the corresponding boundaries may shift with production pathway, composition, and operating conditions.

The working state map therefore links changes in thermal state to heat-transfer performance and reaction onset. This connection is particularly relevant to SAF research because applications in high-thermal-load propulsion systems depend on thermal stability and fuel property evolution across broad pressure–temperature ranges.

In active regenerative cooling scenarios, the fuel must act as a heat sink while maintaining acceptable convective heat-transfer capability under supercritical conditions and enabling subsequent heat absorption through fuel pyrolysis [107]. Existing studies therefore make it increasingly clear that, in active regenerative cooling for hypersonic engines, attention to the supercritical state is a prerequisite for accurately analyzing thermophysical evolution, heat-transfer capability, and subsequent endothermic cracking potential. Experiments on n-decane and RP-3 show that the inlet effect, the buoyancy effect, and the cracking reaction influence convective heat transfer in the inlet region, transcritical region, and cracking reaction zone, respectively [108]. Experimental measurements of heat sink characteristics show that the heat sink augment rate in the cracking reaction region is significantly greater than that in the uncracking region. The same study established a method for defining physical and chemical heat sink, providing data support for the design of regenerative cooling channels [106].

Recent studies have further expanded the understanding of regenerative cooling from simplified straight channel studies toward more realistic multiscale thermal management scenarios [109]. Tian et al. reviewed numerical studies on regenerative cooling with endothermic hydrocarbon fuels and showed that current work increasingly focuses on the coupled effects of transcritical thermophysical properties, fuel pyrolysis, and coke deposition [109]. Their review also indicates that future thermal management studies should strengthen the coordinated modeling of surrogate fuel chemistry, pyrolysis, wall deposition, and turbulence in order to improve the reliability of regenerative cooling analysis [109]. Deep learning has also been introduced into simulations of flow and heat transfer of supercritical hydrocarbon fuels. Li et al. reviewed its use in the solution of flow equations, prediction of mixture thermophysical properties, acceleration of chemical reactions and analysis of macroscopic heat transfer characteristics, while also noting high data dependency and insufficient model generalization capabilities [110].

In addition to straight channels, recent research indicates that the geometry of the channel has a strong influence on the pyrolysis and heat-transfer processes under supercritical conditions [111]. Han et al. [111] reported that in a U-bend tube, secondary flow and secondary reactions considerably affect the temperature distribution, pyrolysis behavior and local heat-transfer effects, which suggests that curved passages can substantially change the regenerative-cooling process [111]. Local resistance measurements for RP-3 flowing in serpentine micro-tubes provide related hydraulic evidence because bend numbers, bend diameters, and bend distances affect elbow pressure drop and local resistance coefficients near the pseudo-critical temperature region [112].

Structural optimization of cooling channels has become an important research topic [113]. Wang et al. showed that simple cubic truss structures could enhance the convective heat-transfer effect and reduce thermal stratification in regenerative cooling channels, indicating that the cooling efficiency is related not only to the fuel properties but also to the channel structural design [113]. Material selection also influences the thermal and structural performance of regenerative cooling channels. Zhang et al. [114] reported that C/SiC increased the calculated thermal safety margin from 21.45% to 39.70% in an RBCC combustor model. The C/SiC–GH3536 hybrid configuration also improved utilization of the chemical heat sink and suppressed local stress concentrations.

At the system level, recent studies have further extended regenerative cooling analysis toward coupled simulations of cooling channels and combustor thermal environments [115]. Zhou et al. demonstrated that the matching relationship between solid thermal conductivity and aero-thermal load has an important influence on coupled heat dissipation between the regenerative cooling channel and the supersonic combustor [115]. Thermal protection at the component level provides a related example. Zhao et al. compared active and passive cooled struts in a hypersonic air-breathing engine and showed that the selection of the strut scheme should consider wall temperature, heat input into the strut, and consumed fuel heat sink [116].

In addition, wall material effects should also be considered in practical fuel system environments [117]. Lu et al. reported that metallic materials commonly used in aircraft fuel systems can promote the thermal oxidation of jet fuel, indicating that fuel thermal stability and coking behavior are jointly controlled by fuel chemistry and wall material interactions [117].

Accordingly, future SAF thermal management studies should strengthen the integrated evaluation of fuel composition, supercritical heat transfer, fuel pyrolysis, wall material effects, and structural cooling design to provide more realistic support for the application of SAF in advanced propulsion systems [109,115,117].

At present, some SAFs with high thermal stability or optimized blended formulations appear to exhibit good thermal stability and coking resistance and may even outperform conventional jet fuel in terms of system efficiency improvement. In particular, predictive models for SAF under supercritical conditions remain insufficient, especially for convective heat transfer, heat absorption through fuel pyrolysis, coupled physicochemical processes, and heat sink behavior over wide pressure–temperature ranges.

6. Conclusions and Outlook

6.1. Summary of the Application Value of SAF

Existing studies identify SAF as one of the most practical near-term technological pathways for aviation decarbonization. Its main advantage is the ability to use existing aircraft, engines, and airport fuel systems, giving SAF a deployment advantage over liquid hydrogen, all-electric propulsion, and some hybrid electric concepts.

Its climate benefit is mainly realized over the life cycle rather than through a large reduction in direct combustion emissions. The magnitude of this benefit depends on feedstock origin, conversion route, hydrogen source, electricity mix, and system boundary.

From an institutional point of view, ICAO has incorporated SAF into international aviation carbon-reduction frameworks and has defined requirements for life cycle emission reduction and sustainability. Therefore, SAF is not only a fuel technology option but has become part of aviation carbon governance practice.

Available engineering studies support the feasibility of SAF use in aviation propulsion systems, provided that fuel specifications and certification requirements are met. Studies on physicochemical properties, spray combustion, thermal stability, coking resistance, and material compatibility suggest that many SAF candidates can be integrated into existing propulsion systems, although performance varies with pathway and composition.

6.2. Current Key Technical Bottlenecks

Although SAF has important application value, its large-scale deployment is still constrained by technical, industrial, and regulatory obstacles.

One limitation lies in fuel composition. Different SAF production pathways result in varying amounts of n-paraffins, iso-paraffins, cycloalkanes, and aromatics, which affect density, cold flow properties, spray combustion, thermal stability, and material compatibility.

Another limitation concerns model development and property prediction. Traditional empirical mixture rules cannot accurately describe the nonlinear behavior of complex fuel mixtures. Molecular simulation and machine learning techniques are promising but require more experimental data, suitable training sets, and stricter uncertainty quantification.

The third difficulty relates to materials and sealing. Low aromatic content is common in most major SAF production routes. While this feature can reduce soot and particle emissions, it may also weaken the swelling required by conventional rubber seals in fuel systems. Material compatibility therefore remains an important issue, especially for high-concentration and 100% SAF application.

The fourth difficulty stems from policy, standards, and economics. Unstable feedstock supply, incomplete refining infrastructure, high production costs, long certification timelines, and fragmented sustainability standards continue to hinder SAF commercialization.

The fifth difficulty concerns application in high-efficiency propulsion systems. In high-thermal load systems, SAF must satisfy conventional combustion requirements while maintaining high thermal stability, resistance to coke formation, suitable flow and heat-transfer behavior, and potential endothermic cracking capability under supercritical conditions. Further fundamental research on these coupled processes is necessary.

6.3. Future Research Directions

Future SAF research should accelerate the shift from empirical property estimation to data-driven and mechanistic prediction. Priority should be given to multi-property models that combine artificial intelligence and machine learning with molecular dynamics, compositional analysis, and experimental databases, so that density, viscosity, flash point, thermal stability, and high-temperature thermophysical properties can be predicted more reliably.

For 100% SAF adaptation, more work is needed on sealing strategies under low-aromatic or aromatic-free conditions. Key tasks include developing new sealing materials, conducting long-term immersion and aging tests, assessing compatibility among fuel system components, and establishing corresponding certification procedures.

For hypersonic and other high-thermal load propulsion systems, SAF should be studied more systematically in active regenerative cooling. Key topics include thermophysical properties in transcritical and supercritical states, heat sink capacity models across broad operating ranges, coupling between pyrolytic heat absorption and convective heat transfer, and coke deposition behavior.

For production technologies, future pathway optimization should give greater weight to cost control, including reductions in energy use and capital cost and tighter control of final fuel composition.

At the standards and industrial levels, further progress is needed in 100% SAF testing, airworthiness certification, and international standardization. SAF evaluation should gradually shift from pathway approval with fixed blending limits toward performance-based methods that emphasize fuel performance and system compatibility.

Future SAF research should therefore move beyond asking whether SAF can replace conventional jet fuel. The next stage should integrate molecular fuel design, property prediction, material selection, thermal management, and certification around the requirements of specific aviation propulsion systems.

text:
Speaking before parliament’s tourism and aviation committee on Wednesday—chaired by MP Sahar Talaat Mostafa, in the presence of Deputy Chairpersons MP Amr Darwish and MP Hesham Hussein, Committee Secretary MP Ahmed El-Ashmouni, along with committee members and several civil aviation officials—El-Hefny said recent fare increases, particularly on return flights from Gulf countries, were driven by “exceptional operational conditions”, including rerouted flights, one-way operations with low load factors, and higher fuel, insurance and operating costs.

He said EgyptAir was honouring its contractual obligations to passengers despite the pressures.

The meeting focused on the state of the aviation sector, including passenger services, pricing, and preparations for the upcoming Hajj pilgrimage.

El-Hefny said a new terminal at Cairo International Airport would raise capacity to more than 60 million passengers a year, part of a broader push to position Egypt as a regional aviation hub.

He also outlined plans to expand and modernise the national carrier’s fleet, with EgyptAir expected to add 34 aircraft to reach a total of 97 by 2030-31.

Air Cairo, a state-affiliated low-cost carrier, is set to double its fleet from about 41 aircraft to 82 over the next four years, the minister said, adding that it currently carries about 20 percent of inbound tourists to Egypt and roughly 30 percent of arrivals at Hurghada airport.

On sustainability, El-Hefny said solar power was already in use at airports in Cairo and Alexandria, with plans to expand nationwide.

He emphasized that environmental challenges are now at the forefront of the global aviation industry, amid efforts to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2050, a goal adopted by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) as part of its global sustainability strategy.

El-Hefny added that Egypt was working to increase the use of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and explore local production to cut emissions and reduce reliance on conventional fuel.

He also announced the cancellation of the paper “passport card” for Egyptian passengers at departure and arrival halls across all terminals at Cairo International Airport, replacing it with a fully integrated digital system in cooperation with the Ministry of Interior, to simplify procedures, accelerate processes, and improve the travel experience.

He added that this system will be gradually rolled out across other Egyptian airports in the coming phase, in line with the state’s broader digital transformation strategy.

El-Hefny underscored that training and qualifying human resources is a core pillar of the sector’s development strategy, contributing to improved performance and enhanced aviation safety and security systems.

Officials also reviewed operational plans for the Hajj season, including the operational plan for EgyptAir and Cairo International Airport, raising operational readiness levels and ensuring full coordination among relevant authorities to guarantee smooth flight operations and high-quality services for pilgrims.

For their part, MPs commended the Ministry of Civil Aviation’s efforts in developing the sector, particularly in updating the legislative framework.

They highlighted the importance of Decision No. 333 of 2026 amending the executive regulations of the Civil Aviation Law, noting its role in improving the investment climate and supporting digital transformation.

At the conclusion of the meeting, the minister reaffirmed the continued implementation of a comprehensive strategy for developing the civil aviation sector, based on sustainability, institutional modernization, and maximizing operational efficiency.

He also stressed the importance of the oversight and legislative roles in supporting the ministry’s efforts, noting that ongoing coordination between the executive and legislative authorities is essential for advancing development, providing a flexible and investment-friendly legislative environment, and achieving the objectives of Egypt’s national Vision 2030 while enhancing the efficiency and sustainability of the civil aviation system.

text:
From waste to oil to end product

The company's value chain starts where the CO2 is: large plants and refineries, currently its primary customers. Dimensional Energy takes captured CO2 or certain other carbon-based waste, converts it into syngas and produces renewable oil products from it.

From there, the oil reaches industries looking to move away from fossil fuels — including producers of sustainable aviation fuel, renewable diesel, lubricants, coolants and specialty waxes and chemicals used in cosmetics, packaging, adhesives and coatings.

Dimensional Energy works with its clients in several ways. It licenses its patented technologies separately or together for commercial projects that transform multiple types of carbon-based waste. It sells oil and renewable fuels directly to clients. It also consults with clients on implementation, including partnering on projects in which its engineers work alongside client teams.

Why Tucson

Dimensional Energy's primary technology center is at the University of Arizona Tech Park, home to the company’s two proprietary systems. They have been operating there since 2022, logging thousands of hours.

One system conditions CO2 into a synthesis-gas feedstock for oil production. The other transforms syngas made from carbon-based waste into new oil products, using feedstocks that can include biogas, wood waste and agricultural residue.

Salfi points to the Tech Park's combination of resources as the draw. The company needed acreage to build a small production facility and now has nearly two acres dedicated to that work. It also relies on the park's laboratory space to develop and test products against specifications, along with the broader business and consulting services available on-site.

description:

In parallel, QNB Group was ranked among Forbes Middle East’s 100 Most Valuable Companies for 2026, reinforcing the Group’s strong market position and institutional strength.
Looking ahead to Q3 2026, QNB Group will continue to build on its strong momentum by advancing a number of strategic priorities.
Backed by disciplined execution, robust governance and a resilient international franchise, QNB Group remains well positioned to capture new opportunities and deliver sustainable long-term growth across its markets.
About QNB QNB Group is a leading financial institution in the Middle East and Africa, operating a diversified international banking platform across more than 28 countries and serving millions of customers worldwide.
text:
CAIRO, Egypt – QNB Group, a leading financial institution in the Middle East and Africa, today issued its Q2 2026 Strategic Progress Update, highlighting continued execution across innovation, sustainability, and institutional capability development across its international network.

During the second quarter, the Group advanced a series of initiatives aligned with its long-term strategic priorities, focused on strengthening economic resilience, supporting future-ready industries, and enabling sustainable growth across key markets.

These developments reflect QNB’s disciplined approach to long-term value creation, underpinned by diversified operations, strong governance, and continued investment in innovation and human capability.

Abdulla Mubarak Al-Khalifa, Group Chief Executive Officer of QNB, said:

“Our Q2 performance demonstrates clear leadership in financing the region's future, from pioneering sustainable energy projects to empowering the next generation of innovators. Our focus remains on supporting economic development, strengthening institutional resilience, enabling innovation, and delivering sustainable long-term value across the markets we serve.

The diversity of our international platform, combined with disciplined execution and strong governance, continues to position the Group to navigate evolving market conditions while maintaining focus on responsible growth and customer-centric innovation.”

Expanding World Capacity Through Strategic Partnerships and Financing

During the second quarter, QNB continued to support strategic sectors and long-term economic development through targeted financing initiatives across its international network.

In North Africa, QNB Egypt participated in the landmark financing of Green Sky Capital's US$500 million Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) facility in Egypt's Suez Canal Economic Zone, the largest SAF production facilities in the Middle East and Africa.. The project is expected to produce up to 200,000 tonnes of biofuel per annum, contributing to an annual reduction of up to 500,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, underscoring our Corporate Banking division's commitment to financing green infrastructure. The project supports the development of future energy solutions while reinforcing the region's role in emerging sustainable aviation fuel value chains

QNB Egypt also signed a medium-term financing agreement worth EGP 5.5 billion with MARAKEZ to support the continued expansion of the District 5 mixed-use development in East Cairo. The project contributes to broader economic activity through integrated residential, commercial, and lifestyle infrastructure.

Further supporting economic development and private sector growth, QNB Egypt signed a credit facility agreement worth EGP 3 billion with GlobalCorp Financial Services Group to support financial leasing and real estate financing activities. The facility is designed to expand access to flexible financing solutions across multiple sectors, supporting investment, business growth, and financial inclusion.

QNB Egypt also successfully arranged an EGP 11.98 billion syndicated loan for Kased Khair for General Supplies and Contracting to finance the development of new marine berths at East Port Said Port. The project is expected to strengthen Egypt’s logistics and maritime infrastructure, enhance trade connectivity, and support long-term economic growth.

The Group also continued to support energy transition initiatives across its international network. In Türkiye, QNB Türkiye provided USD 38 million in long-term financing to support two landmark renewable energy projects. This strategic funding includes USD 23 million dedicated to a state-of-the-art 36MW self-consumption solar power plant, alongside the structured distribution of the remaining USD 15 million – originating from a partnership initiated in 2025 - to partially finance a 140 MW wind power investment. These initiatives showcase QNB’s active leadership in financing sustainable, climate-resilient utility infrastructure globally.

Together, these initiatives support QNB’s broader role in financing projects that contribute to economic resilience, private sector development, and long-term market growth.

Advancing Innovation and Future Capability

The Group continued to strengthen its focus on innovation, education, and future workforce capability through initiatives designed to support knowledge-based growth across the countries we operate in.

During the quarter, QNB partnered with Carnegie Mellon University in Qatar (CMU-Q) to establish the QNB Center for Business Innovation, a platform focused on advancing business innovation, practical learning, and future-ready talent development.

The initiative brings together academic and industry expertise across areas including artificial intelligence, financial literacy, analytics, and leadership engagement, supporting Qatar’s wider ambitions to build a diversified and innovation-driven economy.

In parallel, QNB Group continued to strengthen its long-standing Scholarship Programme, supporting Qatari students pursuing studies across strategic disciplines including technology, cybersecurity, finance, economics, engineering, and business management.

The Group also continued to support the development of future financial sector leaders through international knowledge-sharing initiatives. During the quarter, QNB Suisse hosted a delegation from the Qatar Leadership Centre (QLC) in Geneva, providing participants with insights into global wealth management, sustainable finance, and the evolving dynamics shaping international financial markets. The engagement reflects QNB’s commitment to developing future leadership capabilities and supporting the growth of specialised financial expertise.

text:
Bisnis.com, JAKARTA — PT PLN Energi Primer Indonesia (PLN EPI) mulai membangun ekosistem hidrogen hijau sebagai bagian dari strategi jangka panjang mendukung transisi energi nasional.

PLN EPI membidik pasar hidrogen rendah karbon untuk sektor industri, pembangkit listrik, hingga bahan bakar penerbangan berkelanjutan (electro-Sustainable Aviation Fuel/e-SAF).

Vice President Strategi dan Pengembangan Bisnis Biomassa PLN EPI Anita Puspita Sari mengatakan hidrogen menjadi salah satu pilar dalam peta jalan Net Zero Emissions (NZE) PLN Group 2060.

Setelah mengembangkan bioenergi melalui program co-firing biomassa, PLN EPI kini memperluas portofolio bisnis energi primer dengan membangun rantai nilai hidrogen hijau sebagai salah satu sumber pertumbuhan baru.

"Selain terus mengembangkan energi terbarukan, pembangkit nuklir, Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage (CCUS), energy storage, dan Green Energy Super Grid, PLN Group juga menjadikan hidrogen dan amonia sebagai bagian dari strategi jangka panjang untuk mendukung sistem energi rendah karbon," ujar Anita dalam keterangan resmi, dikutip Minggu (26/7/2026).

Menurut Anita, pengembangan hidrogen dilakukan secara bertahap, mulai dari penyusunan model bisnis, pembangunan kemitraan, hingga penyiapan skema komersialisasi. PLN EPI membuka peluang kerja sama melalui Hydrogen Gas Purchase Agreement (HGPA) maupun kerja sama operasi (KSO) dengan mitra yang mengembangkan fasilitas produksi hidrogen.

Melalui skema tersebut, PLN EPI akan berperan sebagai agregator dan penyedia pasokan hidrogen bagi berbagai sektor yang membutuhkan energi rendah karbon.

"Sebagai subholding yang mengelola energi primer, kami melihat hidrogen sebagai komoditas energi masa depan. Peran PLN EPI tidak hanya memastikan ketersediaan pasokan, tetapi juga membangun ekosistem bisnis agar hidrogen dapat dimanfaatkan secara lebih luas oleh PLN Group maupun sektor industri," kata Anita.

Pada tahap awal, PLN EPI menargetkan sektor industri dengan kebutuhan hidrogen yang relatif tinggi, seperti industri pupuk dan amonia, kilang minyak dan petrokimia, industri baja dan logam, serta industri kimia. Sektor-sektor tersebut dinilai berpotensi menjadi pasar awal hidrogen hijau di Indonesia.

Selain menyasar kebutuhan industri, PLN EPI juga melihat peluang pengembangan electro-Sustainable Aviation Fuel (e-SAF). Teknologi tersebut memanfaatkan hidrogen hijau yang dikombinasikan dengan karbon dioksida hasil penangkapan emisi untuk menghasilkan synthetic crude, yang kemudian diolah menjadi bahan bakar penerbangan rendah karbon melalui konsep closed carbon loop.

Anita mengatakan kebutuhan e-SAF diperkirakan terus meningkat seiring berkembangnya regulasi internasional yang mendorong penggunaan bahan bakar penerbangan berkelanjutan guna menekan emisi sektor aviasi.

"Indonesia memiliki potensi besar untuk menjadi pemain penting dalam industri hidrogen hijau karena didukung sumber energi terbarukan yang melimpah. Tantangan berikutnya adalah mempercepat pembangunan ekosistem, penguasaan teknologi, serta menciptakan pasar yang mampu mendukung pengembangan hidrogen secara berkelanjutan," ujarnya.

Dalam peta jalan NZE PLN Group, hidrogen dan amonia diproyeksikan menjadi bagian dari bauran energi jangka panjang. Seiring meningkatnya pemanfaatan energi baru dan terbarukan, pembangkit listrik berbasis gas juga akan dikembangkan menuju pemanfaatan co-firing hidrogen hingga 100% pada 2060 sebagai bagian dari transformasi sistem ketenagalistrikan nasional.

text:
Eni SpA said Thursday it had signed an agreement to acquire OIL! Tankstellen GmbH from Prax Group.

The transaction will give Enilive, Eni's mobility and biofuels business, about 320 service stations across Austria, Denmark, Germany and Switzerland. "Enilive currently operates approximately 5,300 service stations in Europe", the Italian state-backed energy major said in a statement.

"OIL!'s service stations will be integrated progressively into Enilive's network, which combines a traditional offer of energy carriers with an expanding portfolio of lower-emission mobility products such as HVO [hydrogenated vegetable oil] diesel, the biofuel produced from 100 percent renewable feedstocks at Enilive’s biorefineries in Venice and Gela, currently available in about 1,700 stations across Europe", Eni said.

Eni aims to raise its biofuel production capacity to five million metric tons per annum (MMtpa) by 2030, with plans for sustainable aviation fuel to account for over two MMtpa.

Eni added about the OIL! acquisition, "The offer also integrates fast and ultra-fast electric vehicle charging points (developed together with Plenitude On The Road, a company controlled by Plenitude), and a growing range of convenience and food services, including the proprietary Enilive Café convenience format, which is already present in more than 1,200 locations across Europe, of which over 330 are in Germany". Plenitude is Eni's renewable energy arm.

Earlier this year Prax completed the sale of the Lindsey oil refinery and associated assets in the United Kingdom to Phillips 66. The sale, via bidding supervised by the UK government, had been held under court orders to liquidate several Prax businesses.

"The Prax Group’s UK and European Retail business, Upstream and international operations all currently continue to operate outside of insolvency", Prax says on its website.

The divestment to the Houston, Texas-based company consisted of Prax Lindsey Oil Refinery Ltd, Prax Storage Lindsey Ltd, Prax Terminals Killingholme Ltd, Prax Terminals Jarrow Ltd and Prax Downstream UK Ltd, the UK's Insolvency Service said in a statement April 28.

"Of the remaining employees at the sites, 109 have been retained by Phillips 66 Limited, and 55 will be made redundant", the agency said.

A winding-up order was issued against Prax Lindsey Oil Refinery, Prax Storage Lindsey and Prax Terminals Killingholme on June 30, 2025. That was followed by another winding-up order against Prax Terminals Jarrow on July 22, 2025, and against Prax Downstream UK on November 12, 2025.

In a statement January 5, 2026 announcing Phillips 66's winning bid, the Insolvency Service said, "The conduct of the companies' former directors, following the liquidation, remains the subject of an ongoing Insolvency Service investigation".

Prax has not responded to Rigzone's request for comment on the investigation.

authors: Jacob Johnson, Steven Walker, Aaron Bailey
