title: Boeing stock trades lower as cash burn and 737 MAX issues weigh on outlook
description:
Investors following Boeing stock closely also pay attention to the relationship between free cash flow and capital expenditures.
737 MAX and 787 programs drive delivery and margin dynamics Operationally, Boeing's performance continues to hinge on the trajectory of its flagship 737 MAX narrowbody and 787 Dreamliner widebody programs.
Boeing stock thus remains a leveraged play on global commercial aviation and defense spending, with substantial execution risk embedded in its valuation.
Representative product: 737 MAX family remains central A representative product that captures much of Boeing's financial and strategic narrative is the 737 MAX family of narrowbody jets.
Boeing stock price and trading venue context Boeing stock is listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker BA and trades in US dollars, providing deep liquidity and broad access for global investors.
text:
Boeing stock is still grappling with the financial and operational fallout from its 737 MAX and broader commercial aircraft challenges, with the aerospace group (ISIN US0970231058) showing heavy cash burn and limited near-term relief in its latest quarterly figures reported in 2024 according to public company filings and widely cited financial portals. The company remains a key component of major US equity benchmarks via its New York Stock Exchange listing, but the path back to normalized profitability and free cash flow continues to be long and complex for investors tracking Boeing stock.

Revenue around $78 billion and deep loss in 2023

According to Boeing's 2023 annual report as summarized by major investor information sources, the company generated approximately $77.8 billion in revenue in fiscal 2023, modestly higher than around $66.6 billion reported for fiscal 2022, underscoring a gradual recovery in commercial aviation activity and defense programs. This roughly 17% year on year increase in the top line illustrates that demand for aircraft and services is returning, yet the improvement in revenue has not translated into robust bottom line results.

Despite the revenue recovery, Boeing reported a net loss of roughly $2.2 billion for fiscal 2023, compared with a net loss of around $5.1 billion in 2022, indicating that while profitability remains negative, the scale of red ink has narrowed materially over the latest year. The shrinking loss reflects ongoing cost control efforts, progress on resolving past 737 MAX issues, and incremental margin improvement, but also highlights that Boeing is still far from the level of profitability seen before its MAX grounding and the pandemic shock.

On an operating basis, Boeing's core operating margin for 2023 remained negative, with operating loss reaching several billions of dollars, reinforcing the narrative that the company is still in transition from crisis management toward sustainable performance. For investors analyzing Boeing stock, this combination of improving revenue and still-negative earnings is critical because it frames expectations about how quickly the firm might return to generating consistent earnings per share and free cash flow.

Free cash flow near $4 billion shows recovery trend

One of the more positive data points in Boeing's recent financial history is the significant recovery in free cash flow. Publicly available financial data on Boeing shows that the group generated in the region of $4.0 billion in free cash flow during 2023, a sharp turnaround from the negative free cash flow of roughly $3.8 billion recorded in 2022. This swing of about $7.8 billion year on year provides a quantified comparison that demonstrates how delivery normalization and working capital improvements are starting to benefit cash generation.

The recovery in free cash flow is particularly important because it underpins Boeing's ability to reduce its substantial debt load accumulated during the prolonged crisis. As of late 2023, total debt stood at several tens of billions of dollars, reflecting the financing needed to navigate the prolonged 737 MAX grounding and pandemic downturn. A positive free cash flow number near $4 billion offers the prospect of gradual deleveraging over the medium term, though the process will take years given the absolute size of the liabilities.

Investors following Boeing stock closely also pay attention to the relationship between free cash flow and capital expenditures. In 2023, capital spending remained in the low single-digit billions of dollars, ensuring that the company continues to invest in production capacity, safety improvements, and digital capabilities while still delivering net cash proceeds. That balance between investment and cash generation forms a key pillar of any long-run value recovery narrative for the stock.

737 MAX and 787 programs drive delivery and margin dynamics

Operationally, Boeing's performance continues to hinge on the trajectory of its flagship 737 MAX narrowbody and 787 Dreamliner widebody programs. Publicly available delivery statistics for 2023 show that Boeing delivered around 528 commercial airplanes during the year, up from approximately 480 aircraft in 2022, providing a concrete comparison that reflects the gradual normalization of output following earlier production disruptions. The majority of these deliveries came from the 737 MAX line, which is central to revenue and margin generation in the Commercial Airplanes segment.

Within that total, 737 MAX deliveries are estimated in the mid-300s for 2023, climbing from lower levels recorded in 2022 as regulators and airlines progressively cleared backlogs and returned grounded aircraft to service. The increase in MAX deliveries has a direct impact on segment margin, because the 737 program accounts for a substantial share of Boeing's narrowbody revenues and supports economies of scale across its supply chain. However, recurring quality and safety concerns, including well-publicized inspection campaigns on fuselage components, have constrained the pace at which Boeing can raise monthly production rates.

The 787 Dreamliner program, which had previously experienced production pauses due to quality findings, showed signs of stabilization in 2023. Delivery numbers for the 787 rose from low double digits in 2022 into higher double-digit territory in 2023, helping to diversify Boeing's revenue mix toward widebody aircraft and long-haul travel. Each incremental 787 delivered contributes meaningful revenue, often exceeding $100 million per aircraft depending on configuration, and improves fixed-cost absorption in Boeing's widebody factories.

Defense, Space & Security adds stability but faces its own challenges

Beyond commercial jets, Boeing's Defense, Space & Security segment plays a crucial role in stabilizing group revenue. In 2023, segment revenue was reported around $24 billion, only modestly changed from roughly $23 billion in 2022, indicating a relatively stable base of defense and space contracts even as individual programs encounter schedule and cost pressures. This roughly $1 billion increase year on year illustrates that demand for defense systems and space platforms remains resilient amid shifting geopolitical dynamics.

However, margins in Defense, Space & Security have been under pressure due to cost overruns on fixed-price development programs, including tankers and other aircraft. Segment operating results in 2023 showed negative margins on several large contracts, which offset the stability provided by long-term government relationships. For Boeing stock, this means that while defense revenue helps smooth the volatility of commercial deliveries, it does not yet provide the level of profit cushion that investors might expect from such a portfolio.

Looking ahead, the ability of Boeing's defense business to improve program execution and avoid further charges will be a key determinant of overall group margin. With government customers typically emphasizing reliability and cost control over time, incremental improvements in program management could gradually turn the segment into a more dependable contributor to earnings and free cash flow.

Debt load and balance sheet remain heavy after crisis period

The legacy of the 737 MAX grounding and pandemic disruption is most visible on Boeing's balance sheet. Public financial data suggests that Boeing ended 2023 with total debt of roughly $52 billion, only slightly lower than the peak levels above $60 billion recorded in prior years when liquidity needs were most acute. This leaves the company with a substantial leverage burden relative to pre-crisis norms, when net debt was far lower, and constrains flexibility for dividend resumption or share repurchases.

Cash and marketable securities on hand at the end of 2023 are estimated around $20 billion, resulting in net debt of about $32 billion. This net debt figure is important for investors because it quantifies the magnitude of deleveraging still required before Boeing can claim a normalized balance sheet in line with other large industrial peers. The interplay between free cash flow generation of about $4 billion and net debt in the low tens of billions highlights that the turnaround is a multi-year effort, not a quick fix.

Credit rating agencies continue to monitor Boeing's progress, and while specific ratings may vary, the overall message from public commentary is that sustained positive free cash flow, improved margins, and reduced execution risk on major programs will be necessary to support any material upgrade in credit metrics. For Boeing stock holders, the balance sheet trajectory is thus a central part of the investment case and influences the valuation multiple markets are willing to assign.

Market capitalization reflects cautious investor stance

In equity markets, Boeing's valuation embeds both the progress made and the risks that remain. Widely referenced market portals indicate that Boeing's market capitalization has recently hovered in the $110 billion to $130 billion range, significantly below the peak levels above $200 billion seen before the MAX crisis and pandemic but well above the trough around $60 billion reached at the height of uncertainty. This broad comparison underscores how far the company has come from its worst moments, yet also how much recovery investors still demand before restoring pre-crisis valuations.

The current market capitalization, combined with estimates of normalized earnings power once deliveries and margins stabilize, suggests that investors are pricing in a future improvement in profitability but discounting ongoing regulatory, execution, and competitive risks. The valuation therefore reflects a balance between optimism over long-term air travel growth and caution regarding Boeing's ability to fully capitalize on that growth while managing safety and quality with the rigor expected by regulators and passengers.

For an industrial giant with revenue around $78 billion and positive free cash flow near $4 billion in 2023, a market capitalization in the low hundreds of billions of dollars implies a price-to-sales ratio somewhat above 1 and a forward price-to-earnings ratio that depends heavily on the trajectory of future earnings recovery. Boeing stock thus remains a leveraged play on global commercial aviation and defense spending, with substantial execution risk embedded in its valuation.

737 MAX safety culture and regulatory scrutiny shape narrative

The story behind Boeing's financial figures cannot be separated from safety culture and regulatory oversight. The 737 MAX accidents and subsequent grounding led to intense scrutiny from aviation regulators worldwide, including the Federal Aviation Administration in the United States and counterparts in other jurisdictions. Boeing has since implemented numerous design changes, pilot training updates, and software improvements, but regulators continue to monitor ongoing compliance and production quality through inspections and audits.

Publicly available information indicates that regulators have required Boeing to address specific production issues, such as quality findings on fuselage components and wiring bundles, before allowing higher output rates. These constraints influence how quickly Boeing can move from approximately low double-digit monthly 737 MAX production in recent years toward previously targeted levels above 50 aircraft per month. Each increment in production rate has direct implications for revenue, margins, and free cash flow.

In addition, Boeing has had to invest heavily in safety processes, engineering resources, and internal reporting mechanisms to rebuild trust with regulators, airlines, and the flying public. These investments, while essential, also weigh on short-term profitability. For Boeing stock, the key question is how effectively the company can embed these safety and quality measures into its culture and operations in a way that prevents future crises while allowing for efficient production and innovation.

Competition with Airbus and market share concerns

Boeing's commercial performance is measured not only against its own history but also against rival Airbus in the global duopoly for large jets. Delivery data from industry sources indicate that Airbus has outdelivered Boeing in recent years, with Airbus handing over roughly 735 aircraft in 2023 compared with Boeing's approximately 528. This difference in output has direct implications for market share in the crucial narrowbody and widebody segments.

In the narrowbody market, Airbus's A320neo family has maintained a delivery lead over Boeing's 737 MAX, benefiting from fewer production disruptions and strong demand from low-cost and network carriers. The disparity in delivery numbers has translated into a relative advantage for Airbus in fleet planning discussions and potentially in securing new orders, though Boeing continues to win significant contracts in both domestic and international markets.

In the widebody space, the competition between Boeing's 787 and 777 families and Airbus's A350 and A330neo models remains intense. While Boeing's 787 program has resumed regular deliveries after quality-related pauses, Airbus's A350 has carved out a strong position among long-haul carriers seeking fuel efficiency and range. For Boeing stock, the competitive landscape means that investors must factor in not only internal turnaround efforts but also the risk that market share shifts in key segments could influence long-term revenue and margin trajectories.

Commercial Airplanes segment margins and unit economics

Margins in Boeing's Commercial Airplanes segment are heavily influenced by unit cost curves and learning effects on major programs. Public data for 2023 suggests that segment operating margin remained negative, with losses running into the billions of dollars despite higher deliveries and revenue compared with 2022. This indicates that abnormal costs associated with rework, inspections, and out-of-sequence work on 737 and 787 aircraft are still materially impacting profitability.

Unit economics on the 737 MAX program remain a focal point, as each aircraft delivered both contributes to revenue and helps spread fixed costs over a larger base. As production stabilizes and rework declines, Boeing expects unit margins to improve, which should gradually lift segment profitability. However, the path to positive margins is complicated by supplier readiness, regulatory oversight, and the need to maintain rigorous quality standards.

On the 787 program, the resumption of deliveries and gradual ramp-up in production have begun to restore positive unit margins, though program accounting adjustments and residual rework costs still weigh on reported results. For Boeing stock, the eventual normalization of commercial margins is essential if the company is to achieve a sustainable earnings power that supports debt reduction, potential dividend restoration, and a re-rating of the valuation.

Services business provides recurring revenue base

Boeing Global Services, the company's aftermarket and services division, has become an increasingly important contributor to recurring revenue and margin. In 2023, publicly accessible financial information indicates that services revenue approached around $19 billion, up from near $18 billion in 2022, reflecting growing demand for maintenance, parts, and digital solutions as global flight activity rebounds. This approximately $1 billion increase year on year highlights the resilience and growth potential of the services business.

Margins in the services segment tend to be higher than in commercial manufacturing, providing a stabilizing effect on group profitability. As airlines seek to optimize fleet performance and reduce operating costs, Boeing's services offerings, including predictive maintenance tools and supply chain solutions, can generate incremental recurring revenue per aircraft in service.

For investors in Boeing stock, the services segment represents a key long-term asset that can help smooth earnings across economic cycles and provide diversification away from the more volatile program-based revenue of new aircraft sales. The trajectory of services growth and margin thus plays an important role in assessing Boeing's overall earnings quality.

Long-term demand drivers and fleet renewal needs

Despite near-term challenges, the long-term demand backdrop for large commercial aircraft remains supportive. Major industry forecasts, including those frequently cited by Boeing itself in its market outlook publications, project global passenger traffic growth averaging around 4% per year over the next two decades, leading to demand for tens of thousands of new aircraft as airlines renew aging fleets and expand capacity.

This long-term growth is driven by rising middle-class populations in emerging markets, increased connectivity between major economic centers, and the replacement of older, less fuel-efficient aircraft with modern models such as the 737 MAX, 787, and potential future narrowbody designs. For Boeing stock, such structural demand trends underpin the rationale that the company can, over time, regain a more normalized earnings and cash flow profile if it successfully executes on product development and production.

Nevertheless, the pace at which Boeing can convert long-term demand into firm orders and profitable deliveries will depend on its ability to compete effectively with Airbus, address supply chain constraints, and maintain strong relationships with airline customers. The company must also navigate environmental pressures, including regulatory and investor focus on emissions reductions and sustainable aviation fuel adoption.

Environmental commitments and innovation agenda

Boeing has publicly committed to supporting the aviation industry's net-zero emissions goals by 2050, leveraging technology, sustainable aviation fuels, and operational improvements to reduce the climate impact of flying. The company has announced initiatives to ensure that its commercial aircraft can operate with higher blends of sustainable aviation fuel over time, and it collaborates with airlines and fuel suppliers to advance adoption.

Innovation efforts within Boeing, including work on advanced aerodynamics, lightweight materials, and digital design tools, seek to improve the fuel efficiency of current and future aircraft. While such investments add to research and development spending in the near term, they are critical for maintaining the competitiveness of Boeing's portfolio relative to Airbus and potential new entrants.

For Boeing stock, sustained innovation and credible environmental commitments are increasingly important to attract long-term institutional investors who integrate environmental, social, and governance considerations into their capital allocation decisions. The linkage between R&D spending, product performance, and regulatory compliance thus forms an indirect but meaningful component of the equity story.

Management focus on safety, quality, and culture

Leadership at Boeing has repeatedly emphasized rebuilding safety culture and quality practices as a central priority. Management communications and public comments underline the need for employees at all levels to feel empowered to raise concerns, for engineering voices to carry weight in decision-making, and for production processes to prioritize long-term reliability over short-term output targets.

Changes in organizational structure, the creation of new safety committees, and the enhancement of internal reporting mechanisms are part of this cultural shift. While such changes are difficult to quantify numerically, they are crucial in preventing recurrences of the systemic issues that contributed to the 737 MAX crisis.

From an investor perspective, Boeing stock will likely trade at a valuation that reflects confidence in management's ability to sustain this cultural transformation. If markets perceive that safety and quality have been fully embedded into daily operations, they may be more willing to ascribe higher multiples to future earnings streams.

Representative product: 737 MAX family remains central

A representative product that captures much of Boeing's financial and strategic narrative is the 737 MAX family of narrowbody jets. The aircraft is designed to offer improved fuel efficiency, range, and passenger comfort compared with earlier 737 generations, and it targets the heart of the single-aisle market where airlines demand high-utilization, cost-effective aircraft for short and medium-haul routes.

Order books and delivery statistics show that hundreds of 737 MAX aircraft were delivered in 2023, with thousands more on order from carriers worldwide. Each delivery typically represents tens of millions of dollars in revenue and contributes to Boeing's learning curve on manufacturing efficiency.

However, the product's history of safety incidents and subsequent grounding has left a lasting imprint on Boeing's brand, making the company's efforts to ensure robust safety systems and transparent communications with customers critical. In the long run, the 737 MAX family's performance in service, reliability metrics, and customer feedback will be central to Boeing's ability to reclaim a strong position in the global narrowbody market.

Boeing stock price and trading venue context

Boeing stock is listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker BA and trades in US dollars, providing deep liquidity and broad access for global investors. Public pricing data from major financial portals indicate that in recent months the share price has fluctuated in a wide range roughly between $150 and $220, reflecting shifting sentiment as new information about deliveries, safety findings, and cash flow emerges.

At a mid-range share price level of around $185 as observed in 2024, Boeing's market capitalization would sit in the neighborhood of $115 billion to $120 billion based on roughly 630 million shares outstanding, illustrating the sensitivity of overall valuation to changes in the stock price. The relationship between price moves and news flow about production rates, regulatory developments, and financial results remains strong.

For holders and potential investors, Boeing stock thus represents an exposure to both cyclical factors in air travel demand and idiosyncratic factors related to company-specific execution. The combination of high leverage, large order backlog, and critical safety responsibilities makes the equity story complex but closely watched across global markets.

title: Wie aus Tomaten Treibstoff wird - Der Pragmaticus
description:
Die neue Idee klingt sowieso viel spektakulärer: Marlene Kienberger arbeitet nun daran, aus Überresten der Tomatenproduktion und -prozessierung nachhaltigen Treibstoff für Flugzeuge zu machen.
Elf Projektpartner aus sieben europäischen Ländern koordiniert Kienberger als Leiterin des EU-Projekts „ToFuel“, das den Prozess „Tomate zu Treibstoff“ erforschen und optimieren soll.
„Wir würden niemals schöne rote Tomaten verwenden.“ Am Ende des Prozesses könnte irgendwann eine Bioraffinerie stehen, in der dieser nachhaltige Treibstoff tatsächlich erzeugt wird.
Bei der Fermentation können die Lipide gewonnen werden, die danach in einem mehrstufigen Prozess zu Treibstoff umgewandelt werden.
„Im Idealfall sind es sogar negative Emissionen.“ Deshalb kann sich der Prozess nicht nur darauf beschränken, Treibstoff aus Tomatenüberresten zu produzieren.
text:
Marlene Kienberger forscht in Graz daran, aus den Überresten der Tomaten-Produktion nachhaltigen Flugzeugtreibstoff zu erzeugen.

Am Anfang stand ein guter Plan: „Tomaten aus Glashäusern brauchen sehr oft keinen Humus mehr. Deshalb wollten wir uns anschauen, ob wir aus den Tomatenpflanzen, die ja dann nicht benötigt werden, Pflanzendünger machen können“, erzählt Marlene Kienberger vom Institut für Chemische Verfahrenstechnik und Umwelttechnik an der TU Graz. Bloß: „Das hat einfach überhaupt nicht geklappt.“

Nun sind aber Tomaten nach Erdäpfeln das weltweit meistkonsumierte Gemüse, weshalb bei deren Produktion sehr viel Biomasse anfällt. Ein riesiges, brachliegendes Potenzial. Also musste ein neuer Plan her, um das Grünzeug zu verwerten. Die neue Idee klingt sowieso viel spektakulärer: Marlene Kienberger arbeitet nun daran, aus Überresten der Tomatenproduktion und -prozessierung nachhaltigen Treibstoff für Flugzeuge zu machen. Denn als der Versuch scheiterte, Dünger aus den Rückständen der Tomatenproduktion zu extrahieren, dachte sie sich: „Vielleicht kann man das Grünzeug ja fermentieren.“ Und: „Das ging gar nicht so schlecht.“

Die Tomaten dürfen wir weiter essen

Aus den Abfällen der Tomaten konnten mittels Fermentation Lipide gewonnen werden, also Fettstoffe. Und die können in einem nächsten Schritt zu Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) – nachhaltigem Flugzeugtreibstoff – verarbeitet werden. Das ist natürlich alles nicht ganz einfach zu bewerkstelligen. Elf Projektpartner aus sieben europäischen Ländern koordiniert Kienberger als Leiterin des EU-Projekts „ToFuel“, das den Prozess „Tomate zu Treibstoff“ erforschen und optimieren soll. Ganz am Beginn der Kette steht „Mutti“, der größte Tomatenverarbeiter des Kontinents, der Überreste aus seiner Tomatenproduktion und -prozessierung zur Verfügung stellt. Auf keinen Fall soll etwas verarbeitet werden, das auch als Lebensmittel dienen könnte. „Wir würden niemals schöne rote Tomaten verwenden.“

Am Ende des Prozesses könnte irgendwann eine Bioraffinerie stehen, in der dieser nachhaltige Treibstoff tatsächlich erzeugt wird. „Das ist der Traum“, sagt Kienberger – der Weg dorthin ist steinig. Flugzeuge, die mit Tomatenüberresten betrieben werden, das hört sich spektakulär an. Ist es aber auch, aber mit Einschränkungen, erklärt sie: „Bioraffinerien sind eher ein Nischenthema.“ Warum? „Weil die Transformation des Energiesystems die größere Herausforderung ist.“

Also: Das große Ziel ist es, das Energiesystem zu elektrifizieren. Alternativen für fossile Treibstoffe spielen deshalb eine eher untergeordnete Rolle. Das ist auch der Grund, warum aus den Tomatenresten Treibstoff für Flugzeuge, und nicht für Fahrzeuge gemacht wird: „Autos, Züge und zunehmend auch Lkw werden elektrisch, aber an ein Flugzeug mit Batterie glaube ich nicht“, sagt Kienberger. Es ist einer jener Bereiche, in dem die Elektrifizierung an ihre Grenzen stößt.

Kleinvieh macht auch Mist

Aber wie funktioniert der Prozess genau? „Die Biomasse muss zunächst einmal so aufbereitet werden, dass ein mikrobieller Aufschluss passieren kann“, erklärt sie. Extrusion nennt sich der Prozess, der die Biomasse für die Fermentation vorbereitet. Bei der Fermentation können die Lipide gewonnen werden, die danach in einem mehrstufigen Prozess zu Treibstoff umgewandelt werden. Jeder dieser Schritte wird von einem anderen Projektpartner übernommen, der die dafür benötigten Technologien und Geräte hat – die Aufbereitung der Biomasse passiert in Portugal, die Fermentation in Kroatien, die Umwandlung in Treibstoffe in Leoben und so weiter. Hier in Graz wird das Wassermanagement – „eine Bioraffinerie verbraucht generell sehr viel Wasser“ – und die Lipidaufbereitung übernommen.

Am Ende könnte aber das alles in einer Bioraffinerie passieren, die Tomatenüberreste angeliefert bekommt und Treibstoff ausspuckt. „Ganz trivial ist das aber auch nicht“, sagt Kienberger. Die meisten Tomaten werden zwischen Juli und Oktober geerntet – was macht die Raffinerie in der restlichen Zeit? „Wir schauen uns da natürlich auch andere Reststoffe an, Schilfgras etwa.“ Denn dass sich das Projekt auf Tomaten konzentriert, liegt nicht daran, dass die Pflanze irgendwelche besonderen Eigenschaften hätte, sondern an ihrer Masse: Rund 17 Millionen Tonnen Tomaten werden in der EU jedes Jahr geerntet. Immerhin drei Prozent der bis 2030 in Europa benötigten Sustainable Aviation Fuels könnten aus Tomatenüberresten produziert werden. „Kleinvieh macht auch Mist“, sagt Kienberger.

Nose-to-Tail für eine Pflanze

Dazu kommt noch eine weitere Herausforderung: Die Raffinerie muss nachhaltig und CO2-neutral sein, sonst wäre sie den ganzen Aufwand nicht wert. „Im Idealfall sind es sogar negative Emissionen.“ Deshalb kann sich der Prozess nicht nur darauf beschränken, Treibstoff aus Tomatenüberresten zu produzieren. Bei der Fermentation etwa wird CO2 freigesetzt. Dieses freigesetzte CO2 wird Wasser beigesetzt, in dem lipidbildende Algen leben, die es aufnehmen „und die dann gleich wie die Lipide aus der Fermentation zu Treibstoff weiterverarbeitet werden.“

Die Schalen und -kerne, die dem Projekt von Mutti geliefert werden, können zu Tomatenöl gepresst werden und „einzelne Stoffströme werden vielleicht auch als Tierfutter qualifiziert.“ Denn „nachhaltig kann so eine Raffinerie nur werden, wenn mehrere Produkte rauskommen.“ So sollen alle Bestandteile der Tomate am Ende verwertet werden – Nose-to-Tail, nur eben für eine Pflanze.

Ob der Traum der Tomaten-Bioraffinerie tatsächlich irgendwann aufgeht, weiß Kienberger noch nicht. Zufrieden wäre sie aber auch mit kleineren Erfolgen: „Wenn es am Ende des Projekts Leitfäden für Prozesse wie beispielsweise ein smartes Wassermanagement gibt, die auch von anderen verwendet werden.“ Damit Flugzeuge dann vielleicht auch irgendwann mit Paprika-, Erdapfel-, und Zucchiniresten fliegen können.

title: Air Canada and Airbus plan C$13.7M Canadian SAF platform - Travolution
authors: Kate Harden-England, Travel Weekly Group Ltd
description:
Air Canada and Airbus have launched a jointly funded investment platform from Montreal that could reach C$13.7 million (€8.7 million) to finance domestic production of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).
It will target a jointly selected Canadian SAF project with the objective of taking it to a final investment decision.
Air Canada and Airbus say the platform’s full effectiveness depends on an appropriate public policy framework.
Valerie Durand, vice-president of airport Affairs, Corporate Real Estate and Sustainability at Air Canada, said: “Air Canada is proud to help advance aviation’s energy transition in Canada.
Julie Kitcher, Airbus Chief Sustainability Officer and Communications, said: “I want to thank Air Canada for this very important joint sustainability initiative.
text:
Air Canada and Airbus have launched a jointly funded investment platform from Montreal that could reach C$13.7 million (€8.7 million) to finance domestic production of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

The partners say the move aims to lay the foundations for a Canadian SAF industry and expand its use in corporate travel.

The mechanism is a Sustainability Co-Investment Platform. It will target a jointly selected Canadian SAF project with the objective of taking it to a final investment decision.

Air Canada and Airbus say the platform’s full effectiveness depends on an appropriate public policy framework. The companies are already working with federal and provincial governments and are part of the Canadian Sustainable Aviation Fuel Coalition.

Valerie Durand, vice-president of airport Affairs, Corporate Real Estate and Sustainability at Air Canada, said: “Air Canada is proud to help advance aviation’s energy transition in Canada.

Through this joint initiative with Airbus, we are taking meaningful steps toward supporting domestic SAF production, helping corporate customers address the emissions associated with business travel, and contributing to a lower-carbon path for the industry.

With continued industry collaboration and a supportive policy environment, we are confident this momentum can accelerate,”

Separately, Airbus has committed for five years to Air Canada’s Leave Less Travel Programme. Under the agreement, Airbus will purchase the right to claim the emissions reductions associated with more than 60,000 litres of SAF for a portion of its business travel.

Air Canada will track the emissions generated by Airbus employees’ corporate travel and retire the corresponding SAF attributes on its partner’s behalf. The mechanism is intended to stimulate demand for lower-carbon fuel and does not replace direct emissions reductions at source.

Julie Kitcher, Airbus Chief Sustainability Officer and Communications, said: “I want to thank Air Canada for this very important joint sustainability initiative. Decarbonising aviation will require deep industry collaboration and decades of investment in new sources of renewable energy.

"By launching this co-investment platform and making a long-term commitment to Air Canada’s Leave Less Travel Programme, we will help to stimulate the production of, and demand for, SAF in Canada. The country has a vast feedstock potential.

"When combined with a supportive policy framework, it can contribute to the sector’s decarbonisation ambitions and create significant economic growth and job creation.”

The economic stakes are significant. A study commissioned by Airbus and carried out by consultancy ICF estimates that producing enough SAF domestically to meet 40% of Canadian aviation fuel demand by 2040 could contribute C$32 billion to GDP and create 140,000 jobs across agricultural, forestry and urban sectors.

However, the projections depend on sustained and supportive public policy. Both parties reiterated the aviation sector’s objective of reaching net-zero carbon emissions by 2050.

title: Tecnam reveals first details of the new Rivale aircraft - AvioRadar
description:
Italian aircraft manufacturer Tecnam used this year’s EAA AirVenture Oshkosh to provide the first look at its new personal aircraft programme.
Instead of presenting a conventional mock-up or a computer-generated image of the entire aircraft, Tecnam brought a sculpture made from approximately 1,360 kilograms of stainless steel to Oshkosh.
Tecnam claims that the Rivale will become the first aircraft equipped with Garmin’s new G2000 Prime avionics suite.
The Rivale announcement comes as Tecnam marks 75 years of aircraft manufacturing and engineering.
The company says that more than 8,200 Tecnam aircraft are currently operating in more than 65 countries.
text:
Italian aircraft manufacturer Tecnam used this year’s EAA AirVenture Oshkosh to provide the first look at its new personal aircraft programme. The new model will be named the Tecnam Rivale, with the company so far revealing its name, the forward section of the design and several key technical elements.

Instead of presenting a conventional mock-up or a computer-generated image of the entire aircraft, Tecnam brought a sculpture made from approximately 1,360 kilograms of stainless steel to Oshkosh. Shaped, welded and polished over several months, the structure presents the basic lines of the future aircraft’s forward section.

The steel sculpture was combined with the aircraft’s actual engine cowling, housing a Continental engine from the CD-300 series, and a specially adapted propeller produced by MT-Propeller. Visitors were therefore shown only approximately the first metre of the aircraft, while the cabin, wings, tail surfaces and the remainder of the design remain concealed.

Tecnam plans to progressively reveal additional details, technical solutions and design elements over the coming months. The complete aircraft is expected to be publicly unveiled in 2027.

According to the information released so far, the Rivale will be powered by a six-cylinder Continental engine from the CD-300 series, designed to use Jet A and sustainable aviation fuel. Tecnam says the powerplant has been specifically selected and adapted to meet the requirements of the new programme.

Another major feature will be the cockpit. Tecnam claims that the Rivale will become the first aircraft equipped with Garmin’s new G2000 Prime avionics suite. Further details regarding the instrument layout, display dimensions and system capabilities have not yet been released, although the manufacturer is promising a cockpit distinguished by unconventional lines and styling.

Continental, Garmin and MT-Propeller are joined in the programme by Beringer, Michelin and CAV. Beringer specialises in aircraft wheel and brake systems, Michelin supplies aviation tyres, while the UK-based CAV is known for the development of aircraft ice protection systems.

According to Tecnam, the name Rivale, meaning “rival”, does not refer to a competing manufacturer. Instead, it reflects the company’s intention to challenge and surpass its own previous aircraft with every new programme. The new model is intended to introduce a different approach to the design of personal aircraft, with an emphasis on styling, the flying experience, performance and comfort.

Tecnam has not yet disclosed key technical specifications such as the number of seats, maximum speed, range, useful load or expected price. However, the choice of the approximately 300-horsepower Continental CD-300 engine points towards a high-performance, premium single-engine aircraft.

The Tecnam Rivale can therefore be expected to compete with the Cirrus SR22T and Diamond DA50 RG, which occupy an important part of the market for fast and technologically advanced single-engine aircraft intended for personal and business travel. Depending on its final cabin configuration, useful load, range and performance, the Rivale could also emerge as a single-engine alternative to the twin-engine Diamond DA42.

Such positioning could be particularly attractive to buyers seeking lower acquisition, maintenance and fuel costs than those associated with a twin-engine aircraft, without making significant compromises in terms of cabin space, comfort, modern avionics and long-distance travelling capability. The Rivale’s precise market position will nevertheless become clearer only after Tecnam releases its full configuration and technical specifications.

The Rivale announcement comes as Tecnam marks 75 years of aircraft manufacturing and engineering. The company says that more than 8,200 Tecnam aircraft are currently operating in more than 65 countries.

At Oshkosh, Tecnam also presented the US premiere of the VIP version of its twin-engine P2012 Traveller, as well as the new 215-horsepower P2010 Gran Lusso, equipped with a factory-certified air-conditioning system.

title: Family office of Henderson Land boss to fast-track Central Asia green energy plans
description:
Henderson Land Development co-chairman and managing director Peter Lee Ka-kit’s family office has fast-tracked its plans in Central Asia, where rich agricultural and natural resources could trigger more than US$1 billion in investments in green energy.
Alan Chan Ying-lung, managing partner of family office Full Vision Capital, told the South China Morning Post that the firm was pressing ahead with investment projects such as sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and smart energy storage and solutions in Kazakhstan’s capital, Astana.
He said trial runs using agricultural waste as feedstock for biofuel were under way, pending the finalisation of agreements that would ultimately involve investments of more than US$1 billion.
“We just started the negotiation not long ago, but the progress has gone so fast that it surprised me,” Chan said on the sidelines of the inaugural Nusa Dua Forum, organised by the SCMP and Indonesian sovereign fund Danantara, on Friday last week.
At the forum in Bali, he revealed that Full Vision’s senior management had made repeat trips to Astana since Peter Lee joined the government’s delegation for the Uzbekistan leg of the trip in early June.

text:
Aviation is widely considered one of the hardest sectors in the global economy to decarbonize. While ground transportation such as cars, busses and motorcycles can shift to electric batteries, commercial aircraft face severe physics constraints as modern batteries are simply too heavy and lack the energy density required to lift a long-haul jet across an ocean. This makes SAF the most critical immediate solution for reducing aviation emissions.

Joko Pranoto, Director of Business Planning and Growth at Pertamina Patra Niaga, stated that the company began developing SAF five years ago, which is well before the market and regulations had taken shape. According to him, this strategy was chosen so Pertamina would be fully prepared when the market matures and the government implements a mandatory bio-jet fuel policy. Pranoto said that "we have already conducted trials with Garuda Indonesia and Pelita Air. In fact, this year we signed a SAF sales contract with an international airline to support flights operating from Soekarno-Hatta Airport and Bali."

SAF development does not rely solely on production facilities. Instead, it requires an integrated ecosystem, ranging from feedstock availability and financing to off-takers and regulatory support.

In alignment with the country's net-zero goals, the Indonesian government set a 1 percent SAF mandate that requires all aviation fuel supplied for commercial flights to contain at least 1 percent bioavtur (SAF) blended into conventional jet fuel starting in 2027. In 2029–2030, this mandate is planned to be increased to a 5 percent SAF blend while the long-term (2060) target involves an increase toward 30–50 percent SAF blending.

Rather than imposing the mandate on all domestic flights immediately, something that would trigger a spike in ticket prices because SAF remains 4 to 6 times more expensive than fossil avtur, the government is focusing the initial 1 percent requirement on international flights departing from Indonesia's two busiest international hubs: Soekarno-Hatta International Airport (located just outside Jakarta) and I Gusti Ngurah Rai International Airport (Bali).

Therefore, to prepare for the planned 1 percent SAF mandate, Pertamina is taking several steps. In terms of production facilities, the Cilacap refinery facility is ready to operate, while co-processing trials are underway at the Dumai and Balongan refineries this year. Meanwhile, regarding feedstock, the upstream supply is being strengthened through external partnerships and internal collection systems. Feedstock involves palm oil derivatives and used cooking oil (via co-processing).

Saleh Abdurrahman, a member of the National Energy Council (DEN), noted that Indonesia has the opportunity to become a key player in the regional and global SAF market due to its abundant raw materials. This outlook is reinforced by growing global demand. For instance, the European Union (EU) mandates that aircraft refueling in the region use a 2 percent SAF blend, a share set to increase in the coming years.

However, Abdurrahman emphasized that significant work remains to ensure the sustainable growth of the bio-jet fuel industry. This includes ensuring the feedstock availability and supply chain reliability, the construction of commercial-scale refinery infrastructure, efforts to lower the production costs that remain relatively high (4 to 6 times higher than conventional jet fuel), and maintaining safety as the ratio of SAF blends in conventional jet fuel increases.

Meanwhile, Bayu Sutanto, Secretary General of the Indonesia National Air Carriers Association (INACA), pointed out that the single biggest challenge remains the expensive price of SAF. This is bound to raise flight costs for the airline operator and air traveler. Therefore, Sutanto urges the government to offer specific incentives such as carbon credits or Value-Added Tax (VAT) exemptions on SAF-blended avtur so the added costs are not borne entirely by airlines or consumers.

text:
For many years, the Flint Hills Pine Bend Refinery in Rosemount has produced a lot of the gas Minnesotans use to drive their cars and trucks, and soon, it will produce sustainable fuel for the airline industry.

Friday morning, business leaders and elected officials held a kickoff event to celebrate the new Sustainable Aviation Fuel Blending Facility.

The facility has the capacity to produce up to 30 million gallons of sustainable aviation fuel, commonly referred to as SAF.

SAF is made from a mix of agricultural products such as corn, soy, and other biomass, as well as cooking oil and animal fat.

The SAF that is produced at this facility will be sent directly to Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport (MSP) through a special pipeline.

MSP officials say flights as early as this summer will be using a blend of jet fuel and SAF.

"It's going to generate immense demand for feedstocks. It's going to create jobs. It's going to grow economies," Delta president Peter Carter said.

One of the biggest roadblocks for SAF has been the cost.

Carter says SAF is about three times more expensive than regular jet fuel.

"We would hope that as the industry grows and develops, that it's at least at parity with jet fuel," Carter said.

Several top-level elected officials across both parties support this idea of growing the industry in Minnesota and becoming a global leader in SAF, including Governor Tim Walz and two of the top gubernatorial candidates, Lisa Demuth and Amy Klobuchar.

"We want to make SAF the expectation and not the exception at airports across America, and it starts right here," Sen. Amy Klobuchar said.

Republican Congressman Brad Finstad also attended the kickoff event Friday. He says the project will help local farmers like his great-grandfather.

text:
NASA-backed researchers have identified five alternative aviation fuels that could help meet rising jet fuel demand over the next 25 years. Their latest analysis argues that expanding beyond conventional Jet A and Jet A-1 could strengthen domestic fuel supplies and reduce reliance on imported oil.

The study comes as airlines prepare for a sharp increase in fuel consumption worldwide. Researchers also point to growing concerns over supply constraints and price volatility in traditional jet fuel markets.

SAF closest to scale

The National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) evaluated sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), liquid hydrogen, liquefied natural gas (LNG), liquefied ethane, and an experimental fuel called Jet X. NASA funded the report, which examines each fuel’s production potential, technical readiness, and infrastructure needs.

Researchers project global jet fuel demand will increase from just over 100 billion gallons in 2025 to 165 billion gallons by 2050. That forecast has renewed interest in fuels that can be produced using domestic feedstocks and electricity instead of imported crude oil.

SAF remains the most mature option in the report. Airlines can already blend it with conventional Jet A fuel at concentrations of up to 50% without modifying existing aircraft or airport infrastructure.

Most commercially available SAF comes from used cooking oil, animal fats, greases, and alcohol-based feedstocks. Scientists are also developing production methods that use algae, biomass, and municipal waste.

More from Energy

See All

Despite reaching the commercial market in 2016, SAF still accounts for only about 1% of global aviation fuel use. High production costs and limited biorefining capacity continue to slow wider adoption.

NLR estimates available feedstocks could eventually support production of roughly 132 billion gallons of SAF annually. That volume would meet about 80% of projected global jet fuel demand in 2050 if production capacity expands.

“The transportation fuel market is a global one,” said Kristi Moriarty, senior vehicle and infrastructure analysis researcher at NLR. Government decisions influence whether companies invest in new SAF plants and production pathways, she added, noting faster deployment would be needed to satisfy future demand.

Cryogenic fuels emerge

The report also examines liquid hydrogen, LNG, and liquefied ethane, which belong to a group known as cryogenic fuels. These fuels must remain in insulated tanks at very low temperatures to stay in liquid form.

None of them can replace Jet A in today’s aircraft. Airports would need new fueling systems, aircraft manufacturers would have to certify new designs, and regulators would need global standards for handling and distribution.

Researchers still see significant long-term potential. Liquid hydrogen offers high energy relative to its weight and produces no carbon emissions during flight, making it attractive for future regional aircraft.

Several aerospace companies are already developing hydrogen-powered aircraft and propulsion systems. The Federal Aviation Administration is also working with NLR to prepare airports for future hydrogen operations.

LNG could provide another lower-cost option because the United States has abundant natural gas resources. Liquefied ethane remains largely experimental, although researchers say it offers greater energy density than LNG and production continues to increase.

Jet X remains experimental

Jet X sits much earlier in development than the other fuels. Researchers are studying new liquid hydrocarbon chemistries that could improve fuel economy, reduce harmful aromatics, improve local air quality near airports, and limit contrail formation.

The report says years of additional testing will be needed before Jet X can demonstrate compatibility with aircraft engines, airport equipment, and fueling infrastructure. Researchers believe continued work across multiple fuel pathways will give the aviation industry greater flexibility as demand continues to rise.

text:
Delta Air Lines and Shell Aviation signed a five-year agreement, running through 2030, to build permanent sustainable aviation fuel infrastructure at five US airports. The deal covers LAX, JFK, Boston Logan, Portland, and Minneapolis-St. Paul. Rather than another one-off fuel purchase, this is a shift toward blending, logistics, and delivery systems built to hold up against fuel market shocks.

>> In Other News: [x](x)

What Did Delta And Shell Just Agree To?

Delta Air Lines, the Atlanta-based carrier, and Shell Aviation, the aviation fuels arm of energy company Shell, announced the five-year agreement on July 15, 2026. The deal runs through 2030 and covers five priority hubs: Los Angeles International (LAX), John F. Kennedy International (JFK), Boston Logan International (BOS), Portland International (PDX), and Minneapolis-St. Paul International (MSP).

Shell will manage both blended and neat, meaning unblended, SAF deliveries at each location. That includes the blending, logistics, and distribution work needed to get fuel from producer to aircraft reliably.

The companies have not disclosed the dollar value or total fuel volume of the agreement. Aviation Week reports that Shell will deliver at least 15 million gallons of SAF to Delta in 2026, with options to scale volume in later contract years as the market develops.

>> RELATED: US SAF Production Hits Critical 30,000 BPD

Why Is This More Than Another SAF Purchase Announcement?

Delta's own language points to a strategy shift, moving away from sporadic SAF buys toward permanent supply infrastructure. The company frames this as a response to recent fuel market volatility, not just a sustainability goal.

Delta Chief Sustainability Officer Amelia DeLuca connected the deal directly to supply security, not emissions targets alone.

That framing matters. Roughly 90% of Delta's carbon emissions come from jet fuel, according to the airline's own reporting. When fuel markets tighten, SAF infrastructure becomes both a decarbonization tool and a hedge against supply disruption at the same time.

Global SAF production is expected to reach about 2.4 million metric tonnes in 2026, yet still cover just 0.8% of worldwide jet fuel demand. Source: IATA, June 2026 estimates.

How Small Is The Current Global SAF Supply?

Global SAF production will cover just 0.8% of jet fuel consumed worldwide in 2026, according to the International Air Transport Association. That's the tension behind this deal: a five-hub infrastructure buildout against a fuel pool that's still tiny.

IATA projects total SAF production will reach approximately 2.4 million metric tonnes in 2026, up more than 26% from 2025, per IATA's June 2026 estimates. Airlines worldwide are expected to spend close to 4.3 billion dollars on SAF purchases this year, IATA reports, reflecting the fuel's higher cost relative to conventional jet fuel.

Year Global SAF Production Share of Jet Fuel Use 2025 (estimate) Approximately 1.9 million metric tonnes 0.6% 2026 (projected) Approximately 2.4 million metric tonnes 0.8%

This is why hydrogen hubs facing policy headwinds and SAF infrastructure deals are getting linked together in industry conversations lately. Both depend on building physical delivery systems years ahead of the fuel volumes actually catching up.

Delta's five-hub buildout won't close that supply gap by itself. But locking in logistics and blending capacity now means the airline is positioned to absorb new supply as producers scale. That's a different bet than simply hoping volumes show up.

Delta and Shell plan to test alcohol-to-jet and power-to-liquid pathways alongside SAF made from fats, oils, wastes, and residues, broadening the fuel sources available under the agreement.

What New Fuel Technologies Are Part Of The Deal?

Delta and Shell will jointly test alcohol-to-jet and power-to-liquid production pathways as part of the agreement. Both are next-generation SAF routes that don't rely solely on used cooking oil and animal fat feedstocks.

Shell has said it will source SAF for Delta from multiple producers, including Montana Renewables, a Great Falls, Montana-based SAF and renewable diesel producer, and Diamond Green Diesel, a renewable fuels joint venture between Valero Energy and Darling Ingredients, according to Aviation Week reporting. Initial deliveries will run on fatty acid, waste, and residue based feedstocks, with alcohol-to-jet and power-to-liquid volumes expected to add supply over time.

Shell's aviation lead, Reema Bari, framed the deal as covering both near-term needs and longer-term fuel innovation.

The deal also builds on ground Delta has already broken. The airline is an anchor partner in the Minnesota SAF Hub coalition, and in 2024 received two shipments of more than 7,000 gallons each of SAF at Minneapolis-St. Paul and Detroit airports, the first SAF deliveries in either state's aviation history.

What is Sustainable Aviation Fuel and how does it work? | Shell (official channel, Sep 2025) – Professional explainer on SAF production, use, and benefits including up to 80% lifecycle emissions reduction, featuring Delta Air Lines as an example user."

How Does This Compare To Other Decarbonization Infrastructure Bets?

Delta and Shell aren't the only players building physical infrastructure ahead of demand. The pattern shows up across carbon capture, clean hydrogen hub development, and now aviation fuel.

SAF production capacity: DG Fuels is building a new plant in Phelps County, Nebraska, tied to agricultural feedstock supply

SAF processing technology: Honeywell is supplying modular units for a large renewable fuels complex in Brazil

Carbon removal infrastructure: direct air capture hub funding remains tied to federal budget decisions

The common thread is timing. Companies are locking in logistics, storage, and delivery capacity now, ahead of the point where feedstock supply and production volume actually catch up. Delta and Shell's five-hub deal fits that same pattern in aviation.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Delta and Shell disclose how much the SAF deal is worth?

No. Both companies have kept the dollar value and total fuel volume of the five-year agreement confidential. Aviation Week reports Shell plans to deliver at least 15 million gallons in 2026, with room to scale in future years.

What is alcohol-to-jet fuel?

Alcohol-to-jet, or AtJ, converts ethanol or other alcohols into jet fuel. It's one of several SAF production pathways beyond the more common used cooking oil and animal fat based methods, and it opens the door to agricultural feedstocks at larger scale.

Which airports are covered under the Delta-Shell agreement?

Five US airports: Los Angeles International (LAX), John F. Kennedy International (JFK), Boston Logan International (BOS), Portland International (PDX), and Minneapolis-St. Paul International (MSP).

Where This Leaves The Rest Of The Industry

SAF still makes up less than 1% of global jet fuel today, sitting at that 0.8% mark IATA projects for 2026. Infrastructure deals like this one won't change that number overnight.

What they do change is readiness. When production does scale, whether through new feedstock-based plants or next-generation pathways like power-to-liquid, Delta and Shell will already have the blending and delivery systems in place at five major hubs. That's the real value of this agreement. It's less about the fuel available today and more about the pipes built for the fuel that's coming.

Biofuels, eFuels and Renewable Fuels

A novel process to produce sustainable marine fuel from biomass

IP: 173.73.221.143

The growing green energy revolution in the oil and gas industry has led to the development of successful novel processes that have resulted in green diesel, green sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and green hydrogen (H2). There is also a need for affordable and low-carbon energy fuel in the marine industry, which provides 70%–80% of goods transported internationally. Consequently, the maritime industry generates significant emissions that have a global impact.

With this in mind, the author’s company has introduced a novel processa for producing green marine fuel from biomass. The biocrude upgrading processa offers a compelling pathway to decarbonize marine transportation fuels utilizing biomass that is abundantly available around the world. One study estimates that > 180 B tons per year (tpy) of solid biomass waste are generated every year.1

Agriculture residue from agriculturally important countries (e.g., the U.S., India, Brazil) is typically burned or discarded, providing minimal value; additionally, the burning of these agricultural residues can lead to drastic environmental pollution. The latest example of this pollution can be observed in several cities across India, where the burning of agricultural waste and winter conditions have resulted in air quality index (AQI) increases as high as 400 μg/m3–500 μg/m3. The AQI remains high and has caused severe health concerns for many citizens, resulting in an indirect impact of billions of dollars in health care costs each year. A tenth of this indirect cost, if invested to convert biomass using the company’s biocrude upgrading processa, can result in sustainable generation of fuels and improve the overall environmental footprint.

Forest residue is also abundantly available in many countries. For example, instead of yearly wildfires across North America that burn thousands of acres of forest, this forest residue can be used to generate green and sustainable fuels, contributing to a cleaner environment. Forest residue and agricultural waste are just two examples of how the author’s company’s biocrude upgrading processa can help generate sustainable and green fuels and decrease the industry’s environmental impact.

Regulatory frameworks within the European Union (EU), such as the FuelEU Maritime mandate and EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), have set ambitious targets and are driving the development of alternate fuels in the marine industry to reduce maritime greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and avoid costly penalties across the industry.

FuelEU Maritime is an EU regulation mandating the gradual decarbonization of the maritime sector by setting GHG intensity reduction targets for ships at EU ports. It also requires onshore power supply (OPS) for container and passenger ships, starting in 2025 with a 2% GHG cut, accelerating to 80% by 2050, and introducing port power use from 2030. This law, part of the EU's Fit for 55 packages, applies to ships > 5,000 gross tonnage and covers "well-to-wake" emissions, promoting cleaner fuels and technologies to meet EU climate goals.

The EU ETS is the world's first and largest "cap-and-trade" carbon market, setting a limit (cap) on total GHG emissions from heavy industry, power generation and aviation, and requiring companies to surrender permits (allowances) for each tonne of carbon dioxide (CO2) they emit. It works by setting a declining cap, auctioning allowances and allowing companies to trade them, creating a carbon price that incentivizes cost-effective emissions reductions and funding green projects. The EU ETS is expanding to include shipping, buildings and road transport (ETS2).

In addition to EU mandates, individual countries have set specific GHG mandates. Germany’s GHG reduction quota is a market-based instrument, mainly for the transport sector, which requires fossil fuel suppliers to reduce their average emissions over time. Under current regulations, the quota mandates that fuel suppliers must reduce emissions by a legally specified percentage. The obligation increases annually, reaching a total reduction of 25% by 2030. Companies can meet these targets by using lower-emission fuels like biofuels or electricity, or by purchasing GHG reduction certificates (GHG quotas) from other entities, such as owners of electric vehicles or public charging station operators.

The author’s company’s biocrude upgrading technologya converts forestry waste and agricultural waste into drop-in or blended fuels to produce a cost-effective and lower carbon alternative to traditional heavy oil fuels. This renewable marine fuel can also extend a maritime vessel’s range without expensive engine upgrades.

Many existing renewable fuel technologies are constrained by limited feedstock availability, but the proprietary biocrude upgrading processa unlocks access to billions of tons per year of underutilized solid biomass waste globally. This significantly expands the potential supply of sustainable fuels for the future and reduces dependence on fossil fuels. A significant advantage of this process is that in addition to marine fuel as a main product, this technology can also produce SAF that can be used as both aviation fuel and gasoline fuel for automobiles. This improves the carbon footprint of industry and reduces emissions. The company’s technologya is flexible and can be modified according to customer needs based on varied feedstocks available as well as product needs (e.g., SAF, green marine fuels, green naphtha).

The author’s company’s biocrude upgrading technologya starts with the thermochemical conversion of lignocellulosic biomass into a biocrude intermediate often referred to as crude pyrolysis oil. This crude pyrolysis oil is then upgraded to stable products (e.g., renewable gasoline, SAF, renewable marine); additionally, this process includes deoxygenation and hydrotreating steps. Due to favorable operating conditions (operating temperatures and pressures), the process does not involve high cost and hard-to-fabricate metallurgy (alloys, hastelloys, etc.). Rather, it relies on carbon-steel and in some areas stainless-steel metallurgy for equipment, thereby improving its cost-effectiveness. The technologya is also flexible and can use existing units (retrofitted and/or revamped) to generate green fuels. The maritime industry can now embrace green technology and transition to cleaner fuels, helping lower global emissions as outlined in the FuelEU Maritime Mandate and EU ETS.

The author’s company provides process technologies for renewable and alternative fuels using various feedstocks. The new biocrude upgrading technology is complementary to some of the company’s renewable fuels portfoliob,c,d,e.

NOTES

a Honeywell UOP’s Biocrude Upgrading

b Ecofining™

c Ethanol-to-Jet (ETJ) technology™

d Fischer-Tropsch (FT) Unicracking™

Aspen-based nonprofit Climate Curve honored 10 climate solution teams at its inaugural awards ceremony on July 1 at the Paul JAS Center, held in partnership with XPRIZE. On his first-ever visit to Aspen, late-night host and Emmy winner Seth Meyers emceed the gala, which drew scientists, entrepreneurs, investors and advocates for an evening organizer Jacquelyn Francis described as proof that climate work can be “inspiring, collaborative and even fun.”

Guests enjoyed cocktails and passed hors d’oeuvres in the open-air setting before being seated for dinner and the awards ceremony.

The 10 Keeling Curve Prize winners were narrowed down from 20 finalists, themselves selected from a pool of more than 600 applicants worldwide, with two laureates emerging in each of five categories. In the carbon sinks category, Airbuild, Inc. of the U.S. builds self-powered systems that use microalgae to clean polluted water while pulling carbon from the air, producing biochar as a byproduct, while the National Indian Carbon Coalition helps Indigenous and Tribal nations in the U.S. and Canada strengthen forest health while accessing environmental funding on their own terms.

On the energy side, Switzerland’s Barefoot College International trains women in remote, often under-resourced communities to become solar engineers, bringing clean power to their villages, and Singapore’s Flint Paper Battery is developing rechargeable batteries from cellulose, zinc and manganese as an alternative to mined lithium and cobalt. The finance category went to the U.S.-based Delta Institute, which works to make soil carbon a standard factor in how Midwest farmland is valued, and the Global Heat Reduction Initiative, which translates climate science into data that shapes real investment and mitigation decisions.

For social and cultural pathways, Social Capital Initiatives helps rural Asian communities design local projects that earn exchangeable credits for training and small-business support, while the Farmlink Project connects farms with surplus food to communities facing hunger, cutting both waste and the methane it generates. Rounding out the winners in transport and mobility, LanzaJet produces non-oil-based sustainable jet fuel at commercial scale, and Kenya’s LinQ Powr refurbishes retired EV batteries into backup power systems for East African motorcycle-charging stations.

text:
The Trump administration is studying the deployment of offshore nuclear power generation, with the Marine Minerals Administration and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission agreeing this week to coordinate on any future developments. The announcement comes amid surging electricity demand driven by Big Tech.

“Submerged reactor systems have been safely deployed in naval applications for decades, demonstrating their potential as a reliable source of energy in demanding marine environments. While no commercial deployment on the Outer Continental Shelf is planned or approved at this time, it could greatly strengthen America's energy security in the future,” the acting director of the Marine Mineral Administration, Matt Giacona, said.

The new partnership is part of a broader push to boost the share of nuclear power in the U.S. energy mix, with Reuters recalling in a report that President Trump wants to increase nuclear capacity in the country fourfold by 2050. Indeed, nuclear, which previously fell out of favor because of the high upfront costs and a perception of high risk, has recently been regaining that favor because of its zero-emission principle of operation and the fact that it supplies baseload power.

That last fact has really tipped the scales in favor of nuclear as Big Tech emerges as the main driver of global electricity demand growth because of its focus on artificial intelligence development and application. The industry—just like every other, and households—needs a reliable power supply, and that means either baseload from hydrocarbons or nuclear, or wind and solar plus batteries, with battery technology still not advanced enough to secure the 24/7 uninterrupted supply necessary for data center operators.

Nuclear is making a return, but floating nuclear generation specifically is not really a popular technology globally, yet. There is only one offshore nuclear power station in operation, and that is Russia’s Akademik Lomonosov, which was built to power the Far Eastern Chukotka Peninsula and Yakutia regions. The station began commercial operation in 2020 and was recently reported to have generated its first billion kilowatt-hours.

Related: India Targets Five Small Modular Reactors by 2033

The facility works with reactors similar to those used in Russian nuclear-powered icebreakers, and Rosatom, which built the station, plans to build four more and export the technology, offering plant capacity of 100 Mwe and a service life of 60 years.

China is also working on floating nuclear power generation. One company recently unveiled plans to build a nuclear-powered offshore logistics hub that would produce zero emissions, including through using nuclear fuel for powering ships.

It seems interest in offshore nuclear is growing, with two recent news reports about companies working on the technology. One of these is a U.S. startup by the name of Bluecore Energy, which is developing small modular reactors that can be deployed on floating barges and supply electricity to ports and other infrastructure, Baird Maritime reported this week.

In another report from this week, Samsung Heavy Industries was named as a signatory of a partnership deal with another U.S. company, Sargent & Lundy, for the development of small modular reactors for floating offshore power generators. The deal would see the Korean heavyweight develop a small modular reactor standard platform, following its development of a conceptual design for such a facility. In short, floating nuclear, which was mocked by some when the Akademik Lomonosov was launching, has now become an interesting avenue of energy exploration.

Yet not all in the U.S. federal government are fans of offshore nuclear. The Interior Department, for instance, has national security concerns related to the technology, with Reuters citing the agency as noting radar interference as one specific problem. Environmentalists, separately, believe offshore nuclear power generation is “a terrible idea” that would harm marine life.
